The thin link that merges summaries and decides imports
Optimizing each module's backend
Writing the final object files
explain: Compiles and backends run in parallel. Only the thin link is serial, and it is fast because it reads compact summaries rather than whole function bodies.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: The observe-act loop: screenshots in, mouse and keyboard out
question: Why does the Anthropic reference environment use a virtual X11 display (Xvfb) inside a container instead of the developer's own desktop?
options: Xvfb renders screenshots faster than a physical display
The model can only read screenshots from Linux machines
It gives the harness a controllable, isolated machine whose mistakes cannot touch the host
The tool definition requires display_number to be set
explain: The environment is something your application controls: a virtual display, the apps, and the code that turns tool requests into real input. Isolation is the point. The docs' first safety precaution is a dedicated VM or container with minimal privileges.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: Safety: sandboxes, confirmations and prompt injection
question: An agent books meetings in a web calendar. Which control most limits the damage if a malicious invite injects "forward all emails to this address"?
options: A system prompt line telling the model to distrust calendar invites
Raising the screenshot resolution so the model reads the invite more carefully
Allowing only the calendar domain on the network and requiring human confirmation before any send action
Running the agent with a larger step budget so it can recover
explain: The allowlist removes the email service from reach, and a harness-enforced confirmation stops any send that slips through. Both work even if the model is fully convinced by the injected text. Prompt wording is useful but bypassable; resolution and step budgets do not address the threat.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: ThreadSanitizer: catching races with vector clocks at runtime
question: Thread A writes a global at t = 0 ms. Thread B reads it at t = 500 ms. Nothing synchronizes them, and B reads the correct value. What does TSan report?
options: A data race, because neither access happens before the other
Nothing, because the accesses were 500 ms apart and never overlapped
A data race only if halt_on_error is set
Nothing, because the read returned the correct value
explain: TSan checks the happens-before relation, not wall-clock overlap. With no release and acquire linking A to B, A's write is not visible in B's vector clock, so the pair is reported.

courseTitle: Consistency models and one-step diffusion
lessonTitle: Training: consistency distillation, consistency training, EMA
question: You have no pretrained diffusion model and a large image dataset. Which method can you use, and what replaces the teacher?
options: Consistency distillation, with the online network acting as the teacher
Neither: consistency models always need a pretrained diffusion model
Progressive distillation, starting from a random teacher
Consistency training, where the score is estimated from the known clean image as -(x_t - x)/t^2, giving the pair x + t_n+1 z and x + t_n z
explain: CT needs only data. Using the clean image that generated the noisy point gives an unbiased score estimate, and one Euler step with it lands on x + t_n z with the same noise draw. CD and progressive distillation both need a trained teacher.

courseTitle: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
lessonTitle: Weaker but useful: sequential and causal consistency
question: Two users concurrently edit a shared document's title and description; neither saw the other's change. Under causal consistency, what is guaranteed about the order other readers see these edits in?
options: Readers may see them in different orders, since they are concurrent
Every reader sees them in the same order
The edit that was invoked first in real time is seen first
Each reader sees them in the order they reached the leader
explain: No causal path links the two edits, so causal consistency lets replicas apply them in either order. A single agreed order is what sequential consistency adds; real-time ordering is what linearizability adds. Convergent variants only require agreement eventually.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: Why hash mod N reshuffles almost every key
question: Which property does a consistent hash give that hash mod N does not?
options: Keys are spread evenly when the server set is fixed
Adding a server moves keys only onto the new server, never between existing servers
Every key is stored on more than one server
Lookups need no hash function at all
explain: Both schemes spread keys evenly for a fixed set of servers. What consistent hashing adds is monotonicity: when a server is added, the only keys that move are those that now belong to it. Replication is a separate choice layered on top.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction: hard filters, then soft scoring
lessonTitle: Elasticsearch bool: filter context versus query context
question: An engineer writes `bool: { filter: [work_auth US], should: [skills go, skills rust] }` meaning "authorized AND (Go OR Rust)". What does the query actually return?
options: Authorized candidates who know Go or Rust
Authorized candidates, with Go and Rust only raising the score; candidates with neither are still returned
Nothing, because should requires all clauses to match
Candidates who know Go or Rust, whether authorized or not
explain: Because a filter clause is present, minimum_should_match defaults to 0 and the should clauses are optional. Fix it with "minimum_should_match": 1, or move a nested bool with the two should clauses into the filter list.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: Backtracking search with forward checking and MRV
question: Why does MRV pick the variable with the fewest remaining values first?
options: That variable is the most likely to cause a failure, so the search finds dead branches near the top of the tree
It makes each node cheaper to expand because there are fewer values to loop over
It guarantees the first solution found is optimal
It keeps more values available for the other variables
explain: MRV is fail-first. Every variable must be assigned anyway, so tackling the most constrained one early exposes dead branches high up, where pruning removes the largest subtrees. Option D describes LCV, the value-ordering rule, which aims at success instead.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: CP-SAT in practice: lazy clauses, models and statuses
question: You run the same CP-SAT model twice on an 8-core laptop with default parameters and get two different optimal schedules with the same objective. What is the most likely reason?
options: A bug: optimal solutions must be unique
The second run hit a time limit
Presolve removed constraints differently on the second run, making one schedule invalid
The default uses all cores, and parallel workers race, so which optimum is reported can vary between runs
explain: Several schedules can share the optimal objective. With num_workers at its default of 0, CP-SAT uses all cores, and whichever worker finds a solution first in a given run can differ. Both answers are correct; set num_workers = 1 (and a fixed seed) when you need repeatable output.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Pinning by digest, signing images and verifying at admission
question: Why does keyless signing reduce one big risk of classic signing?
options: It makes signatures shorter
There is no long-lived private key to steal; each signature uses a short-lived certificate tied to an OIDC identity and recorded in a public log
It does not need a network
It hides who signed
explain: Classic signing depends on guarding one private key for years. Keyless signing ties each signature to an identity at that moment, and the transparency log lets identity owners spot misuse.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: RBAC: roles, bindings and the permissions that escalate
question: Which grant gives a user the ability to run commands in any pod on a node, without appearing in the API audit log as pod exec?
options: list on configmaps
create on events
get on nodes/proxy
get on pods/log
explain: nodes/proxy reaches the kubelet API, including exec. The good-practices page says it bypasses audit logging and admission control, and that even the get verb is enough because websocket requests are authorized as get.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Secrets: base64 is not encryption
question: An EncryptionConfiguration lists providers in the order identity, aesgcm. New Secrets are written. Are they encrypted in etcd?
options: Yes, with aesgcm
No: the first provider encrypts new writes, and identity means plain text
Only Secrets created by admins
Yes, with both providers
explain: The guide says if identity is the first provider, at-rest encryption is not enabled. The second provider is only tried when reading data it previously wrote.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a hardening map and where to practise
question: A team can do one thing this week on a cluster with no network policies, Baseline pod security, and ingress-nginx admission webhooks. Which change shrinks the most attack paths from a single compromised pod?
options: Enable debug logging
Rename the default service account
Switch base images to distroless
Default-deny network policies with explicit allows, including restricting the webhook to the API server
explain: Under default allow, any pod can reach every service, admin webhook and node port. Default deny turns one foothold into a contained one and directly blocks the IngressNightmare path. Distroless helps too, but only for the images you rebuild.

courseTitle: Containers and Kubernetes: namespaces, cgroups and scheduling
lessonTitle: Kubernetes: pods, requests versus limits, and placement
question: Nodes have 3800m allocatable CPU and 14592Mi allocatable memory. Free right now: node-a 1500m and 7592Mi, node-b 800m and 11992Mi, node-c 2000m and 2092Mi. A pod requests 1000m and 6144Mi. Which nodes are feasible?
options: node-a and node-c, because both have enough CPU
All three, because no limits were set
node-b and node-c, because each has the most of one resource
node-a only
explain: Filtering needs every requested resource to fit at the same time. node-b fails on CPU (800 < 1000) and node-c fails on memory (2092 < 6144), so only node-a clears both and scoring has one candidate. Having plenty of one resource does not help when the other is short, which is how a cluster ends up with idle CPU and nowhere to put a pod.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: The filters object and its four update operations
question: The user says *any seniority is fine*. Which state change is most faithful to what they said?
options: Leave level as it was (carryover)
Set level to null
Set level to dontcare
Reset the whole state
explain: Null and dontcare both remove the filter, but dontcare also records that the user answered the question. A system that later asks *which level?* would be asking something already answered. Carryover keeps the old filter, which is the wrong behavior here.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Plausible is not faithful: the biasing-feature test
question: Turpin et al. measure unfaithfulness only on examples where the biasing feature points to a wrong answer, using the accuracy drop. Why does that subset make accuracy a usable metric?
options: Because on that subset any answer that follows the bias is wrong, so bias-driven flips show up as lost accuracy
Because models never follow biases toward correct answers, so those examples carry no signal
Because CoT only exists on examples the model gets wrong
Because accuracy on that subset equals the fraction of CoTs that mention the bias
explain: When the bias points to a wrong option, following it costs accuracy, and the authors verified that almost all of the drop is extra bias-consistent answers rather than random noise. The bias does also push toward correct answers on the other subset (accuracy rises there). The metric says nothing directly about mentions; mentions were checked separately (1 of 426).

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: CoT monitors, and what training against them does
question: A team trains with reward = (tests pass) - penalty x (monitor flag). Flag rate falls from 30% to 2% while test pass rate rises. Which check best distinguishes real improvement from obfuscation?
options: Check that the CoTs still read fluently and stay on topic
Measure hacking with a signal independent of the CoT, such as reverting test edits or a held-out action check
Ask the trained model whether it is hacking
Re-run the same CoT monitor with a higher temperature
explain: Obfuscated CoTs are fluent and on topic by construction, and the trained policy is optimized against this monitor, so rerunning it adds little. Asking the model trusts the very channel in question. Only a behavior measure that does not route through the CoT (like Baker's revert-the-test-edits check) can reveal hacks the monitor no longer sees.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: The naive loop: four stages, one at a time
question: Someone optimizes the kernel from 24 ms to 12 ms. What is the new batch time and the new SM utilization?
options: 49 ms, utilization 24.5 percent
30.5 ms, utilization unchanged at 39.3 percent
49 ms, utilization 39.3 percent
37 ms, utilization 32.4 percent
explain: 20 + 16 + 12 + 1 = 49 ms, and the SMs are now busy 12 of those 49 ms, which is 24.5 percent. Halving the kernel bought 19.7 percent of wall time and made the imbalance worse. The 37 ms of host and copy time is where the remaining win lives.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: Two kernels at once: concurrency, stream priorities, comm overlap
question: Same situation, but you create the small kernel's stream with the greatest priority from cudaDeviceGetStreamPriorityRange. What changes?
options: It preempts running blocks and starts at 0.10 ms
It starts at 1.00 ms and ends at 1.25 ms; the big kernel ends 0.25 ms later, at 2.25 ms; the total is unchanged
Both kernels finish sooner, because a high-priority stream raises the SM clock
Nothing, because priorities apply only to memory copies
explain: Priorities "do not preempt already-running work", so the small kernel still waits for wave 1. When SMs free up at 1.00 ms its waiting blocks are preferred, so it finishes at 1.25 ms. The big kernel's last 20 blocks start 0.25 ms later. Priority reorders the queue; it does not add capacity.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: In an inference server: double buffering and reading the gaps
question: You add `print(loss.item())` inside the step loop of an otherwise well overlapped pipeline. What does the profile look like?
options: Unchanged; printing is host-only work and overlaps with the GPU
Slightly slower, by the cost of one small device to host copy per step
The CPU blocks every step waiting for the GPU, the pipeline drains, and per-step gaps appear; it would also make the region uncapturable as a graph
The kernels get slower because the host competes for PCIe bandwidth
explain: `.item()` synchronizes the CPU with the GPU, so the host stops issuing ahead and the pipeline empties every step. PyTorch's notes list CPU-GPU synchronizing ops such as `.item()` as prohibited during graph capture for the same reason. This is the classic accidental barrier, alongside a stray default-stream copy.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Why a reranker reads the query and the document together
question: A team wants to replace their bi-encoder with a cross-encoder for first-stage retrieval over 20 million passages. What is the core problem?
options: Cross-encoders cannot handle passages longer than a sentence
Every query would need 20 million transformer forward passes, because no document computation can be done ahead of time
Cross-encoders need the documents to be pre-embedded with the same model first
Cross-encoders only work with BM25 candidates
explain: The cross-encoder's document token states depend on the query, so nothing can be precomputed. Scoring a full corpus means one forward pass per document per query, which is why it is used only on a shortlist from a first stage.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: From [CLS] to a score: logits, sigmoid and monoT5's true token
question: In monoT5, why does ranking by the softmax over all vocabulary tokens work poorly compared with the two-token softmax?
options: Because the vocabulary softmax is too slow to compute
Because probability mass on thousands of unrelated tokens varies across inputs and swamps the true versus false comparison
Because T5 cannot output the word true
Because the vocabulary softmax is not differentiable
explain: The paper reports near-zero metrics for that variant. Restricting to the two target tokens turns the output into a clean binary decision, sigma(z_true minus z_false), that is comparable across candidates.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Choosing a reranker and using its scores: domains, languages, cutoffs
question: A teammate sweeps alpha from 0 to 1 on all 300 SciFact test queries and reports the best value, nDCG@10 0.708, as the interpolated system's score. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, because alpha is a single parameter
Interpolation must use raw logits, not min-max normalized scores
nDCG@10 cannot be used to choose alpha
The score was tuned on the same queries it is reported on, so it overstates what new queries will get; choose alpha on held-out queries or cross-fit
explain: Choosing the best of 11 settings on the test queries picks up their noise. Cross-fitting chose alpha on one half and scored the other, giving 0.704, a little lower than 0.708 and the number to report.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: The one-time pad: perfect secrecy and the cost of reusing a key
question: Why does a one-time pad not replace AES for HTTPS (encrypted web traffic)?
options: Because XOR is too slow on modern CPUs
Because the key must be as long as all the traffic and delivered securely in advance
Because it was broken by quantum computers
Because it cannot encrypt binary data
explain: The pad is unbreakable but its key logistics are impossible at internet scale. Practical ciphers use a short key (16 or 32 bytes) and accept security based on computational difficulty.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Hash functions: fingerprints, avalanche and the birthday bound
question: Roughly how many random inputs until a collision is likely for a 160-bit hash such as SHA-1, if the hash were ideal?
explain: Birthday bound: about 2^(n/2) = 2^80. Real attacks on SHA-1 do better than that by exploiting its structure.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Randomness: where keys come from, and the Debian disaster
question: Which Python call should generate a password-reset token?
options: random.getrandbits(128)
secrets.token_urlsafe(32)
uuid.uuid1()
hash(time.time())
explain: secrets reads the OS CSPRNG. random is predictable from its state or seed, uuid1 encodes time and the machine address, and hashing the time adds no entropy.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Putting it together: TLS 1.3 and the rules of using crypto
question: A teammate proposes encrypting session cookies with AES-CTR and a counter stored in memory that resets to 0 on restart. Which rule does this break?
options: Do not hash passwords
Never reuse a nonce: after a restart the same counter values repeat under the same key, and CTR also lacks authentication
Use constant-time comparison
Retire SHA-1
explain: A counter that resets repeats keystreams (two-time pad), and plain CTR gives no integrity, so cookies could be bit-flipped. Use an AEAD with random or persistent nonces, or a vetted token library.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Bleichenbacher and ROBOT: retiring RSA key exchange
question: A legacy appliance only supports TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA and the vendor will not patch it. Which action addresses the risk best?
options: Add a random delay to its TLS error handling
Switch the appliance to a 4096-bit RSA key
Enable more cipher suites so clients avoid RSA
Move the service behind a TLS terminator that offers only ECDHE with AEAD suites, using a key the appliance never holds
explain: Random delays average out, and a longer key does not change the padding oracle. Terminating TLS in front of the appliance with modern suites, and a key the appliance does not share, removes the vulnerable code path. ROBOT noted some appliances could not be used securely at all.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Secret-dependent timing: comparisons, Minerva and TPM-Fail
question: Why did a leak of only the bit-length of k, a few bits per signature, lead to full key recovery in Minerva?
options: Because lattice techniques combine small leaks from hundreds or thousands of signatures into the full key
Because the bit-length reveals the private key directly
Because the smart card also reused k
Because the leak let the attacker read memory
explain: Each signature known to have a short k carries a little information about the private key; lattice methods combine many such signatures to solve for it. The paper reports 500 to 2,100 signatures, depending on the noise.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Reviewing crypto code: safe APIs, tests and migration
question: A review finds `Cipher(algorithms.AES(key), modes.CTR(nonce))` with `nonce = os.urandom(16)` and no MAC, used to encrypt session data stored in a cookie. Which change addresses the most important problem?
options: Use a 32-byte nonce
Replace it with an AEAD such as AESGCM or Fernet so modified cookies are rejected
Switch CTR to CBC
Base64-encode the ciphertext
explain: The random 16-byte CTR nonce is acceptable for uniqueness; the missing integrity is the real flaw, since the client holds the cookie and can modify it. CBC is also unauthenticated, and encoding changes nothing.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: From MMA atoms to TiledMMA and TiledCopy
question: A TiledMMA uses the SM80 16x8x16 FP32-accumulate atom with a 2x2 layout of atoms (4 warps) and no value repetition. How many FP32 accumulators does each thread hold?
explain: Each atom is one warp computing 16x8 = 128 accumulators over 32 threads, so 4 per thread. A 2x2 layout of atoms adds more warps, not more values per thread: 128 threads cover 32x16 = 512 accumulators, still 4 each.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: CXL protocols, device types and the path of one load
question: A vendor ships a card with a CXL controller and 256 GB of DRAM and no compute engine. Which protocols must it implement?
options: CXL.cache only
CXL.io and CXL.mem
CXL.io and CXL.cache
CXL.mem only, because CXL.io is optional
explain: This is a Type 3 memory expander. It needs CXL.io for discovery and configuration (every device does) and CXL.mem so the host can load and store its memory. It has no cache of host memory, so CXL.cache is not needed.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Placing pages: tiering in Linux, pooling in Pond
question: Pond allocates a VM's predicted untouched memory from the pool and exposes it as a zero-core NUMA node. Why the zero-core node rather than mixing pool and local memory in one node?
options: Because CXL memory cannot be part of a node that has CPUs
Because the guest OS then prefers its local node and touches the pool only when it needs more, so correctly predicted untouched memory costs nothing
Because hypervisors cannot map CXL memory into guest page tables
Because it makes the pool memory persistent
explain: With a uniform address space the guest would scatter allocations across pool and local memory. A CPU-less node is a fallback in Linux's default policy, so the guest fills local memory first; if the untouched-memory prediction is right, the pool slices are never touched.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: View source is not hacking: the Missouri teachers' SSNs (2021)
question: A reporter views page source on a public US state website and finds exposed personal data. Which risk does the Missouri case show remains even after Van Buren?
options: None: Van Buren makes all viewing of public pages legal everywhere
Only copyright claims
Only a civil CFAA suit
A broader state computer crime statute and public accusations, even if no gate was broken
explain: Van Buren interprets one federal statute. State laws such as Missouri's 569.095 use different words, including 'intentionally examines information about another person'. The prosecutor declined, but the case shows the risk is real.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Copyright and trade secrets: DMCA section 1201 and Megamos Crypto
question: In Volkswagen v Garcia, what mainly concerned the court, as CyBOK describes it?
options: That the researchers had sliced the chip
That the algorithm was weak
That the algorithm was recovered from third-party software that may have existed through trade secret misappropriation
That the paper was written in English
explain: CyBOK notes the court seemed to accept that recovering the algorithm from the chip itself would raise no case. The problem was the provenance of the software the researchers used.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Professional ethics: ISC2, ACM, the Menlo Report and the UMN patches
question: Which Menlo principle most directly captures the kernel maintainers' main objection to the UMN experiment?
options: Justice
Respect for law and public interest
Respect for persons
Beneficence
explain: Respect for persons is operationalised through informed consent. The maintainers were unwitting subjects of an experiment on their review behaviour.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Excess loss: measuring how much a domain can still be learned
question: Why does DoReMi use a reference model of the same size and architecture as the proxy, rather than a tiny bigram model as DRO-LM did?
options: So the two losses are on a similar scale and their difference is meaningful
Because bigram models cannot compute log-likelihood
To make the reference model share weights with the proxy
explain: The paper says it uses a same-size reference so the losses are on a similar scale. A much weaker reference would leave large excess loss everywhere and blur the signal.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Knobs, failure modes, and what came after DoReMi
question: Two teams run DoReMi on the same corpus, one with a 50k-vocabulary tokenizer and one with a 256k vocabulary, and get noticeably different weights. Is something broken?
options: Yes, DoReMi should be tokenizer-independent
Yes, one of them forgot to average over steps
No, weights are token proportions and per-token losses, both of which change with the tokenizer
explain: Domain weights are defined by token counts and excess loss is per token. Different tokenizers split domains into different numbers of tokens, so the weights legitimately differ. The DoReMi repo calls this out explicitly.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Cleaning the crawl: heuristic rules, perplexity filters, exact dedup
question: After exact and near deduplication, your forum domain shrinks from 20B to 8B unique tokens. You keep its learned weight of 0.04 in a 1T-token run. What changed?
options: Its epochs went from 2 to 5, past the roughly 4 where repetition is nearly free, so recompute the weights or cap the domain
Nothing, because the weight is unchanged
Its epochs halved, because duplicates no longer count
The domain is now read less than once
explain: 0.04 x 1T = 40B tokens. Before dedup that was 40 / 20 = 2 epochs; now it is 40 / 8 = 5 epochs. Dedup removes copies from the data, but a fixed weight brings the repetition straight back through extra epochs.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Worked example: binary search over animation keyframes
question: You double the track to 256 keys but keep the same layouts. How large is the SoA times array, in 64-byte lines?
options: 8 lines
32 lines
64 lines
16 lines
explain: 256 time values at 4 bytes each = 1,024 bytes = 16 lines. The AoS array would be 256 x 16 = 4,096 bytes = 64 lines, still 4 times larger, because each record is 4 times the size of a time.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Finding sensitive data: inventories, patterns, checksums and context
question: Why is the Luhn check useful in a discovery tool even though it offers no security?
options: It can only be computed by the card issuer
It encrypts the number
It cheaply discards about 90% of random digit strings before more expensive context checks
It identifies the card's owner
explain: Luhn was designed to catch transcription errors. Any 15 digits have exactly one valid check digit, so random strings pass only about 10% of the time: a cheap filter that cuts noise before the detector looks for keywords and dates.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Searching encrypted data: deterministic encryption and enclaves
question: What does attestation give a client of a secure enclave?
options: Encryption of data in transit
Evidence, checked before any keys are shared, that the enclave is genuine and runs the expected code
A backup of the column master key
A guarantee that no side channel exists
explain: Attestation is how the client decides the enclave is genuine and runs the expected code. It is not transport encryption or key backup, and it does not prove the hardware is free of side-channel weaknesses.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Where DLP acts: endpoints, email, web and cloud
question: A company wants to stop customer data being uploaded to personal cloud drives. Its web proxy does not decrypt TLS. Where can it still enforce this?
options: Nowhere: TLS makes uploads invisible
At the destination cloud provider's servers
In the email gateway
In the endpoint DLP agent and managed browser, which see the file before it is encrypted for upload
explain: Without TLS interception the proxy cannot see content, but the endpoint agent sees the file and the upload attempt on the device itself, before TLS. That is the 'upload to restricted cloud service domain' activity in Microsoft's endpoint DLP.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a data security programme, and practice
question: A company encrypts every database with TDE, runs DLP on email, and has never run discovery. Which lesson-1 gap remains widest?
options: Data in transit
The databases' backups
Side-effect copies (exports, tickets, shares, buckets) that nobody knows exist, so no control is applied to them
Outbound email
explain: TDE protects the known databases and their backups against stolen media, and email DLP covers one channel. Without discovery, copies elsewhere are unprotected and unmonitored: the Pegasus pattern.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: What Internet honeypots see: noise, bots and reused passwords
question: Two thirds of the passwords bots tried were already in a breach corpus. Which defence does this support most directly?
options: Rejecting passwords that appear in known breach lists
Forcing password changes every 30 days
Hiding the SSH banner
Moving SSH to a different port
explain: Bots mostly replay leaked and default passwords. Blocking breached passwords removes them; forced periodic changes and port moves do little against list-based guessing.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: Deception in Active Directory: honey accounts and honey SPNs
question: Why is "any 4769 event where ServiceName is the decoy" a far better rule than "many 4769 events with RC4"?
options: RC4 tickets are never requested legitimately
Event 4769 is only logged for decoys
No legitimate client ever requests the fake SPN, so the decoy rule has almost no benign matches, while RC4 requests have legitimate sources such as old systems
The decoy rule also blocks the request
explain: Metcalf notes some systems and trusts still use RC4, so the volume rule needs tuning. The decoy turns "potential" into "definite" because only an enumerating intruder asks for it. It detects; it does not block.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: Measuring value: the Tularosa study, metrics and practice
question: Your decoy dashboard shows zero alerts in a year. Which follow-up question matters most?
options: Should we remove the decoys to save money?
Did we test each decoy end to end in that year, and did the test alerts reach a person?
Can we make the decoys produce more alerts?
Are the decoys on the Internet?
explain: Silence is only good news if the decoys demonstrably work. Untested decoys may have been broken for months.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Seeds and RNG state: a different problem from kernels
question: Two requests arrive with the same seed and the same temperature, and the sampler draws from one shared RNG stream. What does request B's token depend on?
options: How many draws the sampler already consumed for other requests, so B's token depends on the traffic around it.
Nothing beyond its own seed, since the seed fully determines the stream.
Only the temperature, because the seed is consumed once at startup.
The order in which atomic adds landed in the final GEMM.
explain: A shared stream makes the position in the stream part of the request's input, and that position is set by the queue. Seeding the stream fixes the sequence of numbers, not which element of it your request receives. Per-request generator state is what removes the dependency.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Why distributed bugs refuse to reproduce
question: Jepsen-style fault injection and DST both inject partitions and crashes into real code. What does DST add that changes day-to-day debugging most?
options: It tests a formal model instead of the code, so it is exhaustive
Any failing run can be replayed exactly from its seed
It needs no changes to how the system does I/O
It runs on real hardware, so timing is realistic
explain: Determinism is the key addition: a failure becomes a seed you can replay, step through and add logging to. DST does test the real code (not a model), it usually *does* require routing I/O through simulated interfaces, and its timing is simulated, not real.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Replaying failures, the limits of DST, and who uses it
question: Which system is the *weakest* fit for designing DST in from the start?
options: A new replicated log written in-house with its own network and disk layer
A large existing service built on many third-party clients, thread pools and direct system calls
A consensus library whose I/O already goes through small traits
A storage engine with a single-threaded event loop
explain: Designing DST in requires every source of nondeterminism to be pluggable, which is hard to retrofit across many dependencies and threads. The Antithesis docs call it generally impractical for systems already in production; that is the case a deterministic hypervisor targets. The other three are close to the FoundationDB and TigerBeetle shape.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Least-privilege pipeline credentials: tokens, environments, secrets
question: A deploy key is stored as a JSON document with three fields in one secret. A tool prints the parsed `private_key` field on error. What happens in the log?
options: It is probably shown: redaction matches the exact stored string, and one field of the parsed JSON is a different string
It is masked, because the whole secret is masked
The job fails before printing
GitHub deletes the log automatically
explain: GitHub warns that structured data makes redaction fail because redaction largely relies on finding an exact match. Store each sensitive value as its own secret.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Reviewing infrastructure as code: reading a Terraform plan
question: A reviewer reads only the HCL diff in a PR, which changes a variable default from `10.0.0.0/16` to a module input. Why should the pipeline also check the plan JSON?
options: The plan JSON holds the resolved values, such as the CIDR the module actually produces, while the HCL only shows a reference
The HCL diff is always longer
Plan JSON is required by Git
HCL cannot contain security groups
explain: Values from variables, modules and data sources are only known after planning. Scanning the plan catches what the source hides behind references.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Sentinel, enforcement levels and guardrails developers accept
question: A new rule would block 40 pull requests a week across the company, and nobody has seen its results yet. Which enforcement level should it start at?
options: Hard mandatory, so the problem is fixed fastest
Advisory, to measure impact and fix false positives before anything blocks
Soft mandatory with no override permission
No policy at all
explain: Advisory is Sentinel's default and lets a policy fail with a warning. Starting there turns the unknown 40 a week into a measured list before teams are blocked.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Why generate text in any order other than left to right?
question: What does the 'absorbing state' in masked diffusion refer to?
options: The final layer of the Transformer that absorbs all positional information
The [MASK] token: once the forward process masks a token, it stays masked
The end-of-sequence token that stops generation
A Gaussian noise vector added to token embeddings
explain: In D3PM's absorbing-state process every token moves to [MASK] at some point and never leaves it. At the final time the sequence is entirely masked, which gives a simple known starting point for generation.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Why parallel decoding breaks, and how to make it fast
question: You set Fast-dLLM's threshold so that, in a hard reasoning span, no masked token reaches it. What does the sampler do?
options: It commits the single most confident token, so it degrades gracefully to one token per pass
It stalls until the model becomes more confident
It commits every token in the block anyway
It restarts the block with a new random seed
explain: The threshold rule always unmasks the highest-confidence token to guarantee progress. In uncertain regions the sampler becomes sequential, which is exactly where dependencies between tokens matter most.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Goodput: requests per GPU that meet both SLOs
question: Your summarization service has a 15 s TTFT SLO and a 0.15 s TPOT SLO. Attainment is failing. Which change most likely helps?
options: Protect decode steps from long prefills (separate decode GPUs or smaller prefill chunks)
Give prefill more tensor parallelism to cut TTFT
Lower the TTFT SLO to 5 s
Batch more prompts into each prefill
explain: With a 15 s TTFT budget, prefill is rarely the binding constraint. The long documents create long prefills that stall decode steps and break the TPOT SLO, which DistServe observed for vLLM on LongBench, a benchmark of long-document tasks. Shielding decode is the fix; batching more prompts would make the stalls worse.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Disaggregation at scale: MoE, expert parallelism and elastic pools
question: After a product launch, prompts get 4x longer while output lengths stay the same. In a disaggregated deployment with a load-based autoscaler, which pool should grow, and which signal moves first?
options: Decode, first seen as rising TPOT
Neither: the P:D ratio depends only on the request rate
Prefill, first seen as queued prefill tokens and rising TTFT; decode KV utilization climbs later as the larger caches arrive
Both equally, first seen as GPU utilization
explain: Prefill work per request grows at least 4x (more with attention), so the prefill share of GPU time rises, as in the 08 to 14 window of the timeline. Requests queue at prefill before anything reaches decode, so queued prefill tokens and TTFT move first, the signal Dynamo's load-based planner watches. Each request also brings 4x more KV, so decode KV-cache utilization rises next and decode may need capacity too.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: What deleting a file really does: a FAT walk-through
question: After deletion, which piece of the PHOTO.JPG directory entry is gone for good?
options: The first character of its name
Its size
Its first cluster number
Its extension
explain: Deletion overwrote only the name's first byte with 0xE5. Size, first cluster and extension remain, which is why tools show deleted names as ?HOTO.JPG or _HOTO.JPG.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Linux ext4: superblock, inodes, extents and the journal
question: With the default data=ordered journal mode, what can the ext4 journal give you after a file is deleted?
options: Possibly an older copy of the metadata block holding the file's inode, with its extents
A full copy of the file's content
Nothing, because the journal is erased on deletion
The user name of whoever deleted it
explain: data=ordered sends metadata, not file data, through the journal. Older inode blocks in the journal can point recovery tools to the content blocks. ext4 does not log who deleted a file.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Shortcuts, Jump Lists, ShellBags and the Recycle Bin
question: The USB stick is lost. What can still show that the user browsed its folder `E:\Q3`?
options: Only the stick itself
The master file table of the laptop's C: drive
SRUM
ShellBags in the user's hives, and LNK and Jump List entries pointing to `E:\Q3`
explain: ShellBags record navigated folders, and LNK and Jump List entries record opened files with their paths and volume serial, all stored on the laptop. The laptop's C: MFT does not index files on E:.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Anti-forensics from the defender's side: what each trick leaves
question: Why does wiping a file often fail to hide that something was wiped?
options: Wiping tools are blocked by NTFS
The wipe overwrites the content but leaves traces such as the tool's execution artefacts and change journal records of the overwrite
Wiped data can always be recovered by carving
Windows keeps a copy of every wiped file in SRUM
explain: SP 800-86 notes wiping is effective at preventing collection of the content itself, so carving does not undo it. But running a tool and rewriting a file leave execution and journal traces. SRUM stores usage statistics, not files.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: DiskANN search: beam width, SSD reads and re-ranking
question: A DiskANN service is limited by SSD IOPS at peak traffic, and p99 latency is comfortably under target. Which change is most sensible?
options: Increase W from 4 to 16
Increase L to raise recall
Lower W toward 1 to cut total reads per query
Turn off re-ranking
explain: Smaller beams waste fewer reads, so each query consumes less of the IOPS budget; latency rises but there is headroom. The repository docs recommend W = 1 for the highest throughput at a fixed IOPS rating. Re-ranking costs no extra reads, so disabling it saves nothing.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: CAGRA: a fixed-degree graph built for GPUs
question: A CAGRA graph built with intermediate degree 128 and graph degree 64 gives too low recall even with large search settings. Per the cuVS tuning guide, what is the build-side knob to try after graph_degree?
options: Lower intermediate_graph_degree
Disable reverse edges
Increase intermediate_graph_degree, giving pruning more choices
Set alpha = 1.2
explain: cuVS suggests tuning itopk_size (the search-time list size, covered in the next lesson) first, then graph_degree, then intermediate_graph_degree if graph quality is still too low. A larger kNN graph gives the pruning step more candidates, at a higher build cost. CAGRA has no alpha parameter.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: Build it: a DPO run from preference data to evaluation
question: Your step-0 loss is exactly 0.6931, but a padding test fails: an example's log-prob changes when it is batched with a longer one. What is the most likely bug?
options: The learning rate is too high
beta is not 0.1
The reference model is not frozen
Pad positions are counted in the summed log-prob, or attention is not masking them
explain: At step 0 policy and reference are identical, so any masking bug cancels and the loss is still ln 2. The padding test is what exposes it: a correct sum over masked response tokens cannot depend on the batch's other rows.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: Failure modes, fixes, and DPO in production recipes
question: During DPO training your margin and reward accuracy climb steadily, but `rewards/chosen` keeps getting more negative and outputs drift toward degenerate repetitions. Which change most directly targets the cause?
options: Lower beta so the model can move further from the reference
Add a term that keeps the chosen log-prob up, such as DPOP's penalty or an NLL loss on chosen answers
Train more epochs so the margin saturates
Remove the reference model to save memory
explain: The pattern is likelihood displacement: the gap widens because both answers fall. DPOP's hinge penalty and Llama 3's NLL term (coefficient 0.2) both directly penalize a falling chosen log-prob. Lowering beta or training longer lets drift continue.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: How dual writes silently diverge, and how to contain it
question: Why does reading changes from the old store's transaction log remove the two-client race?
options: The log is stored on faster disks
The log batches writes, so they arrive together
The new store receives changes in the single order in which the old store committed them
CDC takes a lock on each row while it copies it
explain: The race happens because the two stores order the same writes differently. A log consumer replays one commit order, so the new store ends with the same last value as the old store for every key once it catches up.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: What end-to-end encryption promises, and against whom
question: Spyware on a phone reads Signal messages. What failed?
options: The Double Ratchet
The endpoint: the device was compromised and reads plaintext after decryption
Sealed sender
The server's TLS certificate
explain: E2EE ends at the device. Malware running there sees what the user sees, as in the WhatsApp VoIP and FORCEDENTRY cases. Protocol properties are intact but irrelevant once the endpoint is owned.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: The symmetric ratchet: a new key for every message
question: A thief copies Alice's current sending chain key CK5. Which messages can the thief decrypt?
options: Messages 5 onward in this chain, until new DH input changes the chain
Messages 0 to 4
All messages ever
None, because chain keys are hashed
explain: HMAC is one-way, so earlier message keys stay safe (forward secrecy). Later keys in the same chain follow deterministically from CK5, so they are exposed until a DH ratchet step replaces the chain.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: Safety numbers: checking that the server gave you the right key
question: Alice and Bob verified safety numbers last year. Today Alice's app says Bob's number changed. What is the right reading?
options: Definitely an attack
A bug; ignore it
Either Bob reinstalled or changed device, or someone substituted a key; confirm with Bob over another channel and re-verify
The server rotated its TLS certificate
explain: Identity keys change on reinstall, so a change is often benign, but it is also exactly what a substitution looks like. Only an out-of-band check tells them apart.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: MLS ratchet trees: updating a big group in log n steps
question: Why can a removed member not read the group after the removing commit?
options: The server stops forwarding
MLS deletes their app
Their signature key expires
Every new path secret is encrypted only to nodes whose private keys the removed member never held, since their leaf and path were blanked
explain: The commit rebuilds the path with fresh secrets and encrypts them to the remaining copath nodes. The removed member knows only old, blanked keys.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: When protocols broke: Matrix (2022) and Threema (2023)
question: The Threema Kompromat attack and the Matrix identifier confusion share which root cause?
options: A key or signature valid in one context was accepted in another: no key separation or domain separation
Weak random numbers
Old TLS versions
Short passwords
explain: Kompromat reused one key across registration and E2E messages; Matrix let one signature serve for device IDs and key IDs. Separate keys per purpose and typed labels in every signed or MACed input prevent both.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: Reviewing a secure messenger, and where to practise
question: Which finding is the most serious for a high-risk user population?
options: The app uses AES-256 instead of AES-128
Safety numbers are 60 digits
The app supports MLS
Message history is backed up by default to a cloud where the provider holds the key
explain: A provider-held backup key recreates everything E2EE removed, for the whole history at once. The others are neutral or positive.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Maps: counting, histograms and timing in the kernel
question: You remove the /has_key(@start, tid)/ filter from the timing script. What do you most likely see?
options: Nothing changes
The verifier rejects the script
A few enormous durations near the system uptime, from calls that started before tracing began and read a start time of 0
Every duration becomes 0
explain: Calls already in flight at attach time only hit the return probe. Their @start[tid] reads as 0, so nsecs - 0 equals the time since boot, which pollutes the top buckets of the histogram.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Affine quantization: storing reals as int8 plus a scale
question: Why does the quantization scheme require that real 0 maps exactly to an integer code?
options: Because int8 cannot store negative numbers
Because zero padding and ReLU zeros would otherwise all carry the same rounding error, acting as a systematic bias
Because the scale S must be an integer
Because dequantization divides by zero otherwise
explain: Zero padding inserts many zeros at borders and ReLU creates many exact zeros. If 0 were not on the grid, they would all round to the same nonzero value, a biased error repeated across the tensor. Jacob et al. and the ONNX Runtime docs both call this requirement out.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Edge devices: the doors attackers now try first
question: Why is a VPN gateway often a more valuable target than an employee laptop?
options: It usually has a faster processor
Laptops cannot be attacked over the network
VPN traffic is not encrypted
Anyone can reach it before login, it holds credentials with reach inside, and it usually runs no EDR
explain: The three properties together: pre-authentication exposure, a privileged position (passwords, service accounts, routes inside) and little monitoring. A laptop typically has EDR and must first be reached through phishing.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Ivanti Connect Secure, 2024: chained zero-days and a fooled checker
question: Why did the toy on-box integrity checker report nothing on a backdoored appliance?
options: Its known-good hashes were wrong
SHA-256 is broken
It only checks files in /tmp
The intruder had root and edited the skip list the checker reads from the same device
explain: The manifest was correct. The checker trusted configuration stored on the device it was checking. Volexity found the real attacker adding entries to the ICT's files; CISA later found even the external ICT missed compromises.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Management interfaces: keep the admin door off the internet
question: Which setup meets BOD 23-02 for a firewall's web admin page?
options: The admin page stays on the internet with a long password
The admin page is moved to port 18443 so scanners miss it
The admin page is public but logs every login
The admin page answers only on an isolated management network reached from admin workstations
explain: BOD 23-02 accepts two options: remove the interface from the internet, or put a separate policy enforcement point in front of it. A strong password, an unusual port or logging leave the interface itself reachable.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Overthinking: 901 tokens to say 2 + 3 = 5
question: A reasoning model's response has 5 solutions; the first correct answer appears in solution 1 (60 tokens) and the response is 600 tokens. A colleague says 'truncate every response after solution 1 and nothing is lost'. What does Chen et al.'s data say?
options: Correct: later solutions never change the answer, so truncation is free
Mostly right for easy sets, but on hard sets later rounds sometimes fix a wrong first answer, and the authors keep one reflection round for that reason
Wrong: later solutions are where most correct answers first appear
Wrong: the first solution is usually the longest, so truncating saves little
explain: Over 92% of correct responses are already correct at solution 1, which is why the waste is large. But not 100%: keeping only the first correct solution (FCS) lowered MATH500 accuracy, so their best recipe keeps one extra reflection round (lesson 2).

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Length penalties inside RL: Kimi k1.5 and DAPO
question: You train with the Arora-Zanette reward and GRPO's std-normalized advantages. On prompts where all 8 samples are correct, you double alpha from 0.1 to 0.2. What happens to the advantages in those groups?
options: They double, so the push toward short answers doubles
Nothing: alpha cancels between the deviation and the std, so the advantages are identical
They halve, because the std grows faster than the deviation
They become zero, because all samples are correct
explain: Every reward is $1 - \alpha f_i$, so both the deviation from the mean and the std scale with alpha and the ratio does not. Zero would be right for a correctness-only reward; here the length term breaks the tie. To keep alpha meaningful, use the plain deviation (no std), as Arora and Zanette do.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: One input, many readers: where encoding bugs come from
question: Which situation is a parser differential?
options: A proxy and the server behind it decide differently where an HTTP request ends
A function crashes on an empty string
One library is slower than another at parsing JSON
A parser rejects input that breaks the specification
explain: A differential is two parsers reaching different results from the same input. Speed, crashes on edge cases and strict rejection are not disagreements between two readers.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Unicode normalisation: NFC, NFD, NFKC and NFKD
question: A file name check rejects `/` and `..`, then the code stores `normalize("NFKC", name)`. What is wrong?
options: NFKC can produce `/` and `.` from fullwidth characters after the check has run
Nothing; NFKC only changes accents
NFKC is slower than NFC
NFKC turns file names upper-case
explain: Fullwidth full stop and fullwidth solidus normalise to `.` and `/`. Normalise first, then check the normalised value, then use that same value.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Confusables and homoglyphs: UTS #39 skeletons
question: Why should you not display or store the skeleton as the user's name?
options: Skeletons are a comparison key that can change the visible text, for example m becomes rn
Skeletons are encrypted
Skeletons are always upper-case
Skeletons remove all digits
explain: A skeleton maps characters to look-alike prototypes, which may be different characters or even sequences (`m` to `rn`). Keep the canonical name for identity and use the skeleton only to detect collisions.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: JSON differentials: duplicate keys, numbers and CouchDB
question: A Go service decodes a quantity as a float64 and a Python service as an int. For which quantity can they first disagree?
explain: Doubles represent every integer up to 2^53 = 9007199254740992 exactly. 9007199254740993 is the first integer that rounds (to ...992). The other values are exact in both.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: From antivirus to EDR: sensor, cloud, console and response
question: Ana's laptop runs signature antivirus only. Word starts PowerShell, which downloads nothing to disk and connects to a remote server. Why might the antivirus stay silent?
options: It judges files one at a time, and no file here matches a known-bad signature; the suspicious part is the sequence of behaviours
Antivirus cannot run on laptops that have Office installed
PowerShell disables antivirus whenever it starts
Antivirus only scans email, never processes
explain: Signature antivirus answers a per-file question. Each file here (winword.exe, powershell.exe) is legitimate. The signal is in the relationships: an Office app starting a shell that then goes online. Recording and correlating those relationships is what EDR adds.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Sysmon configuration: include, exclude and rule groups
question: An admin writes `<ProcessAccess onmatch="include" />` with no rules inside, expecting to see every process access. What does Sysmon log for event 10?
options: Every process access
Only access to lsass.exe
Nothing
Only accesses by unsigned programs
explain: An include filter logs only events that match a rule; with no rules nothing matches, so nothing is logged. To log everything you would use an empty exclude filter (which is usually far too noisy for event 10).

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Application control I: allowlisting and AppLocker
question: A path rule allows `C:\Windows\*`. Why is that weaker than a publisher rule for Microsoft-signed binaries?
options: Path rules are slower to evaluate
Publisher rules also block Microsoft Office
Some folders under `C:\Windows` are writable by ordinary users, so anything a user copies there is allowed; a publisher rule requires the file's signature instead
Path rules only work for DLLs
explain: A path rule trusts a location. Microsoft's default-rules page names `C:\Windows\Temp` as user-writable, so a path rule over the Windows folder lets users run their own files from there. A publisher rule trusts a signature the user cannot forge.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: What EDR can and cannot see
question: Which of these would an endpoint sensor on employees' laptops record?
options: A forwarding rule created in cloud webmail from the attacker's own browser
A login to the company VPN appliance
powershell.exe on a laptop opening a handle to lsass.exe
The content of a TLS connection to a web server
explain: Process-to-process handle requests on a monitored host are exactly what sensors record. The webmail rule and VPN login happen on systems with no sensor, and TLS content is encrypted; only metadata such as the destination is visible.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Hart's NALM: steady states, step changes and signatures
question: A 1500 W kettle and a 1500 W space heater (both nearly resistive) live in the same house. Which feature from Hart's pipeline separates them best?
options: Nothing in a single (dP, dQ) step; you need other cues such as typical duration or time of day
Their reactive power steps, since dQ differs
Voltage normalisation, since it rescales each appliance differently
The steady-state tolerance of 35 W
explain: Both are resistive, so dQ is near zero for both and dP matches: the two points land in one cluster. Reactive power only helps when the loads differ in it. Normalisation is applied to the aggregate, not per appliance. Separating them needs extra features such as on-duration or usage patterns, which is why later models add temporal structure.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Why raw strings break filters and joins
question: A team stores only the canonical company ID and discards the raw string to save space. What goes wrong first?
options: Nothing: the canonical ID carries all the information that was in the raw string
Filters become slower because IDs are longer than names
When the matcher makes a mistake or the taxonomy changes, there is no way to audit or re-run normalization on the original input
Fuzzy matching stops working because IDs cannot be compared with edit distance
explain: Normalization is a lossy, model-driven step that will be wrong sometimes and will be improved over time. Keeping the raw string lets you show members what they typed, debug bad merges and re-normalize everything when the alias table or model changes.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Estimating m and u: random sampling, EM and term frequencies
question: You train Splink's EM with the blocking rule `block_on("postcode")`. Why can it not estimate $m$ for the postcode comparison in that pass?
options: Every pair in that pass agrees on postcode, so the data says nothing about how often true matches disagree on it
Postcode is a numeric field, and EM only handles string comparisons
u for postcode was already fixed by random sampling, which freezes m as well
EM can estimate only one comparison per pass
explain: Blocking on postcode forces agreement on it for all compared pairs, so its m would come out as 1 regardless of the truth. Splink excludes the blocking fields and gets their m from another pass blocked on different fields.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Companies and schools: registries, hierarchies, renames and acronyms
question: A recruiter filters on Meta. Should a profile listing `Facebook` for a job from 2015 match, and what data decides it?
options: No: the profile says Facebook, not Meta
Yes, but only if a fuzzy match between the two names is high enough
Yes: both names belong to one legal entity (Q380), so the alias table plus a dated name history map the 2015 string to the same ID
Only if the member edits the profile
explain: Facebook, Inc. was renamed Meta Platforms, Inc. on 28 October 2021; it is the same entity. The link comes from the alias table and name history, not from string similarity, which between `facebook` and `meta` is near zero.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Who runs the tenant: Entra roles, Global Administrator and PIM
question: Why should emergency access accounts be cloud-only and not synced from on-premises AD?
options: Synced accounts cannot hold the Global Administrator role
So that an outage or compromise of on-premises AD or federation cannot block or take over the last way into the tenant
Because cloud-only accounts do not need MFA
Because PIM only works for cloud-only accounts
explain: Microsoft's guidance keeps emergency access for cloud and for on-premises separate, with no dependency between them. If they were synced or federated, the failure they exist for (federation down, AD compromised) would take them down too.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Entra tokens: lifetimes, refresh tokens and revocation
question: An admin revokes a compromised user's sessions at 14:00. The attacker holds an access token for a third-party API (no CAE) issued at 13:50 with an 80-minute lifetime. Until when can the attacker call that API?
options: 15:10, when the access token expires
Indefinitely, because revocation only affects passwords
explain: Revocation invalidates refresh tokens and sessions at once, but an already-issued access token is checked only by the resource. Without CAE, the resource accepts it until expiry: 13:50 plus 80 minutes is 15:10.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Conditional Access in Entra: baselines and the gaps attackers use
question: Your company buys a multitenant SaaS app and grants it an application permission. You license Workload ID Premium. Can a workload identity Conditional Access policy restrict where that app signs in from?
options: Yes, all service principals are covered
No: Microsoft documents that these policies cover only single-tenant service principals registered in your tenant, not multitenant or third-party SaaS apps
Only if the app is added to a group
Only for managed identities
explain: The documented scope is single-tenant service principals registered in your tenant. Multitenant SaaS apps and managed identities are excluded, and group-based assignment is not enforced, so control those apps through their grants and reviews.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: A hardening baseline, an incident runbook, and where to practise
question: After a full on-premises AD compromise, an organisation rebuilds Entra ID security (new admins, revoked sessions) but leaves Entra Connect, PTA agents and the AZUREADSSOACC key as they were. What is the risk?
options: None: the cloud was rebuilt
Re-compromise: whoever still controls the Tier 0 bridges can change synced users, sit in password checks or forge Seamless SSO tickets
Only that sync will slow down
Only guest users are affected
explain: Lesson 11's bridges create or impersonate cloud identities. Until the sync accounts, agents and Seamless SSO key are reset from a clean AD, the attacker keeps a path back into the tenant.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Level-triggered versus edge-triggered, and reading until EAGAIN
question: A level-triggered server registers every connection with EPOLLIN | EPOLLOUT and leaves it that way. CPU sits at 100 percent even with no traffic. Why?
options: EPOLLOUT is invalid without EPOLLET
Idle sockets almost always have send-buffer space, so each one is reported writable on every epoll_wait and the loop never sleeps
epoll_wait ignores the timeout when EPOLLOUT is set
The kernel rescans the interest list on every call
explain: Level-triggered means "report while the condition holds". Writable is true for nearly every idle socket, so every wait returns immediately with work that is not real. Register EPOLLOUT only while you have unsent data (EPOLL_CTL_MOD), or use ET.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Split by query and keep a rotating sealed test set
question: Why does the MS MARCO document leaderboard score every submission on 45 extra queries that never appear on the public board?
options: To give the organizers a held-out check on whether public gains carry over to queries no one could tune on
To raise the total number of evaluation queries so the public score is more precise
Because TREC labels are too expensive to show publicly
To break ties on the public leaderboard
explain: A private set that no participant receives feedback on cannot be adaptively overfit. If teams were climbing the public board by tuning to its queries, their runs would gain publicly and slip on the private queries.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Non-executable memory: the NX bit, DEP and W^X
question: A program is built with NX but not with a stack canary. An overflow replaces the return address with the address of the overflowing buffer itself, which holds attacker bytes. What happens at ret?
options: The injected bytes run, because NX only protects the heap
The return address is restored by NX
ret jumps to the stack, the CPU refuses to execute from a non-executable page, and the process faults
The compiler refuses to compile the overflow
explain: NX does not prevent the hijack; it prevents the hijacked jump from running data. The process faults on the instruction fetch from the stack page. The return address was still corrupted, which is why attackers moved to reusing code that is already executable (next lesson).

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Control-flow integrity: checking where indirect calls land
question: Microsoft CFG allows an indirect call to any function that is a valid indirect-call target. A corrupted function pointer in a Windows program is changed to point at the start of another such function. What happens?
options: CFG terminates the process because the type differs
NX blocks the call
ASLR moves the function so the call misses
The call is allowed: CFG checks the entry point is valid, not that it is the intended function
explain: CFG is coarse-grained: it rejects calls into the middle of functions or to non-code, but any registered entry point passes. Type-based schemes such as Clang cfi-icall narrow this further, and no CFI scheme can choose between two valid targets of the same type.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Sandboxing as a layer: how Android hardened after Stagefright
question: After Android 7, an attacker achieves code execution in libstagefright through a new parsing bug. What do they most likely still need to read the user's camera?
options: Nothing: libstagefright still runs in mediaserver
Only the camera permission from the app manifest
A way around the integer-overflow sanitizer
A second bug to escape the mediacodec sandbox or to attack cameraserver, which alone may use the camera
explain: The parser now runs in a sandbox that SELinux denies camera access. Camera use is confined to cameraserver, so the attacker needs another vulnerability: the containment goal of the redesign.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Why a write steals the whole line: MESI and ownership
question: Which access pattern causes the most coherence traffic on one 64-byte line?
options: Eight threads each read a different 8-byte field
One thread repeatedly writes all eight fields
Two threads on different cores each write their own field
Eight threads read the same field
explain: Reads leave the line Shared in every cache with no ongoing traffic. A single writer keeps the line Modified in its own cache with no one to invalidate. Two writers on different cores each need an RFO before each write after the other one wrote, so the line ping-pongs.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: The setting: data that is not allowed to leave the device
question: Eight hospitals want one shared model and no record may leave any hospital. What is the training objective?
options: Each hospital trains alone and the best of the eight models is shipped
The same pooled average loss as centralized training, written as a sum of per-hospital losses weighted by record count
The unweighted mean of the eight per-hospital losses, since each hospital is one client
A new objective that no centralized training run could express
explain: Federated learning changes who computes, not what is being minimized. The objective is the pooled average loss, which factors exactly into a sum over clients with weights n_k/n. The unweighted mean is a different objective: it would give a hospital with 200 records the same influence as one with 20000.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Non-IID data and client drift: fast convergence to the wrong answer
question: On the skewed split with E = 5, FedAvg flattens out at 1.944 while the optimum is 2.3. What is the single most reliable fix if you must keep that exact data split?
options: Raise the client fraction C so more clients report each round
Train for ten times as many rounds at E = 5
Do less local work per round (smaller E) or correct the local gradients, which both reduce drift
Increase the local learning rate so clients get closer to their local optima
explain: 1.944 is a fixed point, so more rounds change nothing, and all three clients already report every round so C is irrelevant here. Getting closer to the local optima makes the drift worse: that is the E tending to infinity limit of 1.667. Reducing local work or correcting the local direction (FedProx, SCAFFOLD) attacks the actual cause.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: What the server sees: secure aggregation and differential privacy
question: Under secure aggregation with 500 clients in a round, what does an honest-but-curious server learn?
options: Each client's update, but only in encrypted form it cannot use
The sum of the 500 masked updates, from which it can subtract any client it chooses
Nothing at all, including the sum, until a trusted third party decrypts it
The sum of the 500 updates and nothing about any individual update
explain: The functionality is exactly summation: the server learns the sum and no individual contribution. It cannot subtract one client out, because each client's value is covered by masks that only cancel in the full sum, and the per-user mask b_u blocks the attack of falsely declaring a live client dropped.

courseTitle: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
lessonTitle: Paying for density: M_beta compression and two-hop recovery
question: During compression, candidate d is pruned from v's list because it is in H. At search time, under a predicate where d passes but kept neighbor c (which links to d) fails, can the search still reach d from v?
options: No, because c fails the predicate and is skipped
Yes, if c sits beyond position M_beta, because the lookup expands c's list before filtering
Only if d is within the first M_beta entries
Only with ACORN-1
explain: The two-hop expansion reads c's neighbor list regardless of whether c passes; the predicate is applied to the expanded entries. By construction, any pruned node was in H only because some later kept neighbor links to it, and entries past M_beta are exactly the ones the lookup expands.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Fine-grained experts: split each expert into m slices
question: Why is the combinatorial count, not the expert count, the quantity the paper highlights?
options: Because more combinations means more FLOPs
Because routers need at least a billion options to converge
Because GPUs schedule experts by combination
Because each token's computation is a sum over its chosen experts, so more possible subsets means a more precisely targeted mix of knowledge at the same cost
explain: A token's MoE output is the gated sum of its chosen experts. With 120 possible pairs, many different kinds of tokens must share the same pair. With billions of possible 8-subsets of small experts, the token can assemble a closer fit. FLOPs are identical in both designs.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Putting it together: routing in DeepSeek-V3
question: DeepSeek-V3 relies on the bias method yet still keeps a sequence-wise balance loss with alpha = 0.0001. What is the best justification?
options: The bias method does not work without an auxiliary loss
The bias balances load across whole batches; the tiny loss only guards against extreme imbalance within a single sequence, while staying too weak to cause meaningful interference gradients
The loss replaces the bias during the final 500B tokens
It is needed to train the router weights at all
explain: The report calls it complementary: the main balancing is aux-loss-free, and the sequence-wise term exists just to avoid extreme per-sequence imbalance. Its alpha is ten times smaller than the 0.001 baseline used in the loss-free paper. Router weights are trained by the language-modeling loss through the gate values.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: SPI flash, SMM and the write lock LoJax walked through
question: A platform sets BLE but not SMM_BWP, and its SMI handler correctly clears BIOSWE. Why is the BIOS region still at risk?
options: BLE only applies after the OS boots
SMI handlers cannot run on multi-core CPUs
BLE makes the flash read-only, so no risk
BIOSWE becomes 1 before the handler clears it, so a racing writer can land writes in that window
