explain: An idle CPU runs the scheduling path only when it is woken: by select_cpu choosing it, by a kick, or by new work in its local DSQ. Custom DSQs are only read by dispatch callbacks, so an unread queue plus no kick leaves the task stranded.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Measuring and debugging a scheduler
question: After loading your scheduler, SCX_EV_SELECT_CPU_FALLBACK in /sys/kernel/sched_ext/root/events climbs steadily. What does it point to?
options: The scheduler keeps entering bypass mode
Tasks are being inserted without a slice
Your select_cpu returns CPUs the tasks cannot use, and the core silently picks another one
The watchdog is about to declare a stall
explain: The kernel docs define it as ops.select_cpu() returning a CPU unusable by the task, after which the core picks a fallback. Look for a missing check against p->cpus_ptr, the task's allowed cpumask.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Revocation at scale: CircleCI and rotating every secret at once
question: A breach report says secrets were stolen on 22 December, and you finish rotating on 9 January. Which window do you search your own logs for misuse of those secrets?
options: Only 4 January, the disclosure date
From the earliest possible compromise (16 December here) until your rotation finished on 9 January
From 22 December onward
Only after 9 January
explain: Investigate the whole period a stolen copy could have worked: from the earliest date the vendor could not rule out until your rotation completed. CircleCI's own advice was 16 December through the date you rotated.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Key hierarchies in KMS: envelope encryption and rotating the KEK
question: Following Google's DEK guidance, how often should you rotate a DEK?
options: Every 90 days
Whenever the KEK rotates
Never in place: generate a new DEK every time you write the data, so each DEK protects one write
Only after a breach
explain: A fresh DEK per write means there is no long-lived DEK to rotate. KEK rotation does not touch DEKs at all unless you re-wrap them, and re-wrapping changes the wrapping, not the DEK itself.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Rotation without outages: overlap, versions and staged labels
question: In the overlap timeline, when is it safe to remove k1 from the verifiers' key set?
options: As soon as k2 is published
As soon as signing switches to k2
Once the last token signed with k1 has expired
Never; old keys must be kept forever
explain: Tokens signed by k1 keep arriving until they expire. Removing k1 earlier rejects valid tokens (an outage); keeping it forever means a stolen k1 works forever, which is the Storm-0558 failure.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Python: eval, pickle and yaml.load turn data into code
question: A service loads job descriptions from a shared message queue with `pickle.loads(msg.body)`. The queue is internal. What is the best review comment?
options: Fine: internal queues are trusted by definition
Anyone who can publish to the queue gets code execution in the worker; switch to JSON with a schema
Wrap the call in try/except so malformed messages do not crash the worker
Check isinstance(result, Job) after loading
explain: pickle runs code while loading, so whoever can write to the queue controls the worker. try/except and isinstance checks happen after the code already ran. Internal is not the same as trusted: a compromise of any producer would spread.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Log4Shell as a review miss: a logger that interpreted its input
question: You are reviewing a 2013-style patch that adds a new lookup type to a logging library. Which review comment best addresses the risk?
options: Add unit tests that the lookup returns the right value for a valid name
Lookups are evaluated on logged data, so this lets any logged string trigger a network fetch and code load; make it opt-in and never apply lookups to message data
Rename the plugin to make its purpose clearer
Document the new syntax in the README
explain: The danger is not that the lookup works incorrectly but that it works on attacker-controlled data. Tests of the happy path, naming and documentation do not address that. The CSRB said a focused security review of exactly this addition could have found the flaw.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Heartbleed as a diff: reviewing every field of a message
question: Why did Cloudflare's report say `>=` would have prevented Cloudbleed even though the grammar bug would still exist?
options: Because >= is faster than ==
Because a pointer that jumps past the end still satisfies p >= pe, so the parser stops instead of reading on
Because >= prevents the pointer from moving
Because Ragel only supports >=
explain: An equality check only fires if the pointer lands exactly on the end. If it skips over, == is never true. An ordering check is true for every position at or past the end, so it fails safe even when another bug moves the pointer too far.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Rust: FFI boundaries, release-mode overflow and panics
question: Which FFI call is correct for passing a Rust string to a C function that expects a NUL-terminated string?
options: `f(name.as_ptr() as *const c_char)` with `name: &str`
`let c = CString::new(name)?; unsafe { f(c.as_ptr()) }`
`unsafe { f(CString::new(name).unwrap().into_raw()) }` and never free it
`unsafe { f(name.to_string().as_ptr() as *const c_char) }`
explain: A &str or String has no terminating NUL, so C would read past its end. into_raw without a matching from_raw leaks memory, and unwrap panics on interior NULs. Binding the CString to a variable keeps it alive for the call and guarantees exactly one terminator.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: Secure channels at every layer: what each protocol protects
question: An employee connects to the office through a VPN and then opens an old telnet session to a router inside the office. Who can read the telnet password?
options: Nobody, because the VPN encrypts the whole session end to end
Only the VPN provider, which can see inside the tunnel
Anyone who can capture traffic on the office network between the VPN gateway and the router
Nobody, because telnet hashes passwords before sending them
explain: The VPN protects only the stretch from the laptop to the gateway. After the gateway the telnet packets travel in the clear across the office network. SSH would protect the session all the way to the router. Telnet sends the password as typed; it does not hash it.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: IPsec traps: weak PSKs, aggressive mode, NULL and old algorithms
question: Which ESP setting is forbidden outright by RFC 4303?
options: AES-GCM with a 16-byte ICV
NULL encryption with HMAC-SHA-256 integrity
Both encryption and integrity set to NULL
Tunnel mode between two hosts
explain: RFC 4303 allows NULL encryption (integrity only) and, as a MAY, confidentiality-only ESP, but encryption and integrity "MUST NOT both be NULL". Tunnel mode between hosts is unusual but legal.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: Terrapin (CVE-2023-48795): deleting SSH messages by shifting a counter
question: Why is a connection using aes256-gcm@openssh.com not affected by Terrapin?
options: AES-256 has a longer key than ChaCha20
GCM derives its nonce from a separate invocation counter, not from the shifted sequence number
GCM encrypts the IGNORE message so the attacker cannot inject it
GCM connections do not send EXT_INFO
explain: The attacker shifts the implicit sequence number. ChaCha20-Poly1305 and EtM MACs use it in their integrity check, so the shift is invisible. GCM's nonce starts from a key-derived value and counts invocations independently, so it does not line up after the shift.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: Time is a security input: NTP, delay attacks and NTS
question: An attacker on the path between a client and its NTS server cannot break the cryptography. What can they still do to the client's clock?
options: Nothing, NTS makes time synchronisation fully secure
Replace the time in the reply with any value
Replay an old reply to set the clock back by days
Delay packets asymmetrically, shifting the computed offset by up to half the round-trip delay
explain: Delays leave packets authentic, so NTS cannot detect them; the offset error is bounded by half the round trip (MAXDIST/2 at most). Rewriting the time or replaying old replies fails NTS's authentication and request-response matching.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: What security architecture is: where every control sits
question: A team adds a GraphQL endpoint that queries the database directly, while the REST routes all pass through the authorization middleware. Which reference monitor requirement does the new endpoint break?
options: Always invoked
Tamper proof
Small enough to analyse
Open design
explain: The middleware is a reference monitor, and the new endpoint reaches the objects without calling it. Tamper proofing is about attackers modifying the checker; size is about whether it can be reviewed; open design is a separate Saltzer and Schroeder principle.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Brewer-Nash's Chinese Wall, and choosing the right model
question: A hospital wants to ensure that prescription records change only through the pharmacy system's dispensing workflow, with a pharmacist approving what a doctor writes. Which model fits best?
options: Bell-LaPadula
Biba strict integrity
Brewer-Nash
Clark-Wilson
explain: The concern is how data changes: through certified programs (the dispensing workflow) with separation of duty (doctor writes, pharmacist approves). That is Clark-Wilson. Bell-LaPadula is about disclosure, Biba about trust levels, Brewer-Nash about conflicts of interest.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: NIST SP 800-207: the logical architecture of zero trust
question: During a session the policy engine learns that the device is infected and revokes access. Which component carries out that decision?
options: The policy engine itself, by blocking packets
The resource, by logging the user out
The policy administrator, by signalling the PEP to terminate the session
The SIEM, by alerting an analyst
explain: The PE decides and logs; the PA executes, including revoking an earlier approval by telling the PEP to shut the connection. The PEP is what actually terminates the traffic. A SIEM alert alone does not close anything.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Segmentation and microsegmentation, planned from real traffic
question: Why does SP 800-215 put a unique application identity first among microsegmentation prerequisites?
options: Because IP addresses change and are hidden by NAT, proxies, load balancers and moving VMs, so policy written on addresses cannot say which workload is talking
Because identities are cheaper to store than addresses
Because firewalls cannot read IP headers
Because SPIFFE is required by law
explain: Policy should say which workload may call which, and only a verifiable workload identity (such as a SPIFFE ID in a short-lived certificate) survives the address changes of modern infrastructure.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: From a script to a pipeline: the parts of a security automation
question: Enriching one alert takes about 40 seconds of API calls. Which component should do that work?
options: The receiver, before it answers the SIEM
A worker that takes the alert from the queue
The SIEM, before it sends the alert
The chat bot, when the analyst opens the case
explain: The receiver must answer fast (GitHub, for example, gives up after 10 seconds and counts the delivery as failed), so slow work belongs in workers behind the queue. Making the SIEM or chat bot do it couples your pipeline to tools you do not control.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: Rate limits, backoff with jitter, and partial failure
question: Why add jitter rather than using exponential backoff alone?
options: Jitter makes each retry faster
Without jitter the API will not accept the retry
Jitter replaces the need to honour Retry-After
Clients that failed together would otherwise retry together at every step, recreating the overload
explain: Exponential backoff with identical timing keeps failed clients in lock step. Randomising the wait spreads them out. Retry-After, when present, still sets the minimum wait.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: Worked scenario: prompt injection through attacker-written log fields
question: Which change prevents the attacker from closing A-2291 even if the model is fully persuaded?
options: A stronger system prompt telling the model to ignore instructions in alerts
Blocking the phrase ignore previous instructions
Wrapping each field in its own XML tag
Removing the model's ability to close or downgrade alerts, with deterministic rules making those decisions
explain: Only removing the authority holds when the model is persuaded. Prompts and tags lower the odds (and the attacker can write the closing tag); phrase blocklists are rephrased around.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: What security protects: assets and the CIA triad
question: A web shop's product prices are changed by an intruder so that a laptop sells for USD 1. Customers can still browse and buy, and no customer data was read. Which property was violated?
options: Integrity
Confidentiality
Availability
Non-repudiation
explain: The data was improperly modified, which is an integrity failure. Nothing secret was read (confidentiality held) and the shop stayed up (availability held). Non-repudiation is about proving who created data, which is not the issue here.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: How a vulnerability becomes public: disclosure, CVE and NVD
question: Why does the security world need CVE IDs at all?
options: They give every publicly known vulnerability one shared name that scanners, advisories and people can refer to
They encrypt vulnerability details so attackers cannot read them
They rate how dangerous a bug is
They prove the vendor has fixed the bug
explain: A CVE ID is an identifier, nothing more. Severity is CVSS's job, exploitation status is KEV's, and fix status comes from the vendor advisory. One name lets a scanner report, a vendor bulletin and a news story be matched up.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: The attack lifecycle: kill chain and MITRE ATT&CK
question: In ATT&CK, what is the difference between a tactic and a technique?
options: A tactic is the attacker's goal at that step; a technique is a specific way of achieving it
Tactics are for Windows, techniques for Linux
Tactics are legal, techniques are illegal
There is no difference; they are synonyms
explain: MITRE describes tactics as the why (for example Credential Access) and techniques as the how (for example T1552.001 Credentials In Files). One tactic has many techniques.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: What a security leader is for: the CISO's job and reporting line
question: A CISO reports to the CIO. The CIO's infrastructure team owns 40 unpatched internet-facing servers. What is the main governance risk of this reporting line here?
options: The CISO cannot technically scan the servers
The finding about the CIO's own systems may be softened or delayed before it reaches the CEO and board
The CIO is legally barred from fixing servers the CISO has flagged
Reporting to the CIO makes the CISO the owner of the risk
explain: The issue is a conflict of interest in the information path, not technical access. Risk ownership stays with the business or system owner under the Three Lines Model; a direct audit-committee channel is the usual remedy.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Prioritising a portfolio: expected loss removed per dollar
question: An option removes little expected loss per dollar but is required by a signed customer contract. What should happen?
options: Fund it as an obligation, and record why it sits outside the ranking
Drop it; ratios decide everything
Hide it in another line
Ask the customer to remove the clause before deciding
explain: Obligations are funded regardless of ratio, and the reason is recorded so the portfolio stays explainable. The ranking applies to discretionary spending.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Hiring and keeping people: what predicts performance
question: According to Sackett et al. (2022), which method had the highest mean validity?
options: Years of job experience
Structured interviews
Unstructured interviews
Cognitive ability tests
explain: Structured interviews (0.42) ranked first; cognitive ability tests (0.31) were lower than earlier estimates suggested; unstructured interviews (0.19) and years of experience (0.07) were weak.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Personal liability: what the Uber and SolarWinds records say
question: Which part of the SEC's SolarWinds case survived the July 2024 motion to dismiss?
options: Fraud claims based on the public Security Statement's access-control and password representations
Claims that weak cybersecurity violated internal accounting controls
Claims about the December 2020 8-Ks
Disclosure-controls claims
explain: The court sustained claims about the Security Statement and dismissed the others; in November 2025 the remaining claims were dismissed with prejudice by stipulation.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Severity you can defend: scores, context and confidence
question: A report says only: "Severity: 9.8". What is the most important thing missing?
options: Which scale and version produced it (for example CVSS 3.1 base) and whether it was adjusted for this environment
Nothing; 9.8 is clear
The colour of the severity badge
The name of the tester
explain: The CVSS 4.0 specification asks for nomenclature (CVSS-B, BT, BE, BTE) wherever a number appears, because the same bug scores differently by version and by which metric groups were used.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Incident updates when you do not know yet
question: Which incident update sentence best states uncertainty?
options: We judge it unlikely (about 30%) that customer data was accessed; this rests on 60% of logs reviewed, and we expect a firmer answer by 16:00.
The attacker definitely did not reach customer data.
Customer data may have potentially been impacted in some way.
We cannot comment during an investigation.
explain: It gives a word with a number, the basis for the judgement, and when it will improve. 'Definitely did not' overstates, 'may have potentially' is vague, and 'cannot comment' gives readers nothing to plan with.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Presenting to a board: risk, money and decisions
question: Which slide title is best for a board?
options: Ransomware could stop order fulfilment for about 5 days; target 2; closing the gap needs the backup budget on today's agenda
Firewall dropped 4.2M packets from 37 countries
We are fully compliant with all frameworks
Top 10 CVEs this quarter
explain: It names a business outcome, a measured current state, a target and the decision needed. The others are activity, an unfalsifiable claim, or technical detail directors cannot act on.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: STaR and ReST-EM: sample, keep what is correct, fine-tune
question: Your ReST-EM run uses 64 samples per problem, yet 20% of training problems never get a correct sample. Which change gives the model a training signal on exactly those problems?
options: Train for more epochs on the solutions you already kept
Lower the sampling temperature so solutions are more careful
Continue fine-tuning from the last checkpoint instead of the base model
STaR's rationalization: give the correct answer as a hint and keep rationales that reach it
explain: Problems with no correct sample are invisible to the filter; more training on kept data or lower temperature cannot add them. Rationalization samples from a different distribution, p(r | x, y), which can reach the answer. The cost, covered in lesson 5, is more rationales that reach the right answer for the wrong reasons.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Using failures and training the judge: V-STaR, the gap, Meta-Rewarding
question: What does V-STaR train on that STaR throws away?
options: Rationales produced with the answer given as a hint
Human-written solutions from the SFT set only
Preference labels from a stronger model
Incorrect self-generated solutions, paired with correct ones to train a DPO verifier
explain: STaR keeps only correct samples. V-STaR keeps every labeled sample in the verifier's data and builds pairs of correct and incorrect solutions to the same problem, so the verifier learns this generator's typical mistakes.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Why exact-match caches miss, and how a semantic cache matches meaning
question: A colleague sets RedisVL's distance_threshold to 0.2, thinking it is stricter than the default 0.1. What did they actually do?
options: Made it stricter: hits now need similarity of at least 0.98
Made it looser: hits now need only cosine similarity of at least 0.8
Nothing, because the threshold is ignored for short prompts
Switched from cosine to Euclidean distance
explain: It is a distance, so a larger value accepts neighbors that are farther away. d at most 0.2 means similarity at least 0.8. More hits, and more chances to return the answer to a different question.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Build, measure and run a semantic cache on your own traffic
question: In the replay, raising the threshold from 0.85 to 0.95 cut the hit rate from 18.6% to 5.9%, yet with lambda = 5 the cost fell from 1.042 to 0.974. What explains it?
options: The cache got smaller
Embedding costs fell
False hits fell from 4.6% to 0.7% of requests, and each costs 5 LLM calls
The judge model changed its labels
explain: Cost is (1 - h) + lambda f. Losing 12.7 points of hit rate adds 0.127; removing 3.9 points of false hits saves 5 x 0.039 = 0.195. When a wrong answer is expensive, fewer false hits beat more hits.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Other ways to shrink context: RAG compressors and soft compression
question: You only have API access to the target model. Which compression families can you use?
options: Only soft compression, since it gives the highest ratio
None; compression requires the target model's weights
Gist tokens, if you send them as text
Token deletion, extractive and abstractive compressors, because they all output text
explain: Deletion, extraction and summaries produce ordinary text, scored or written by a separate small model you run yourself. Gist tokens and ICAE memory slots are vectors inside a specific model, so they need its weights and fine-tuning.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Validating outbound URLs in code
question: A developer blocks SSRF by rejecting any URL whose text contains "169.254" or "localhost". Why is this weak?
options: It is too slow for production
It blocks legitimate AWS API calls
Python cannot search strings for dots
A string check misses other spellings of the same address, DNS names that resolve to internal IPs, and redirects; the check must run on the resolved destination
explain: Addresses have many textual forms, any domain can point at an internal IP, and a public URL can redirect inward. OWASP's approach validates the resolved IP and pins the connection to it, on top of an allowlist where possible.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Log4Shell: how logging a string ran code
question: An internal Java reporting service never receives traffic from the internet. Was it at risk from Log4Shell?
options: No: only internet-facing servers could be attacked
Only if it ran on Windows
Only if it used LDAP for logins
Yes, if it logged any data that originally came from outside, such as names or headers passed along by other systems
explain: The trigger is a string being logged, wherever that happens. Data entered on a public site can travel through queues and databases and be logged by an internal Java service later, which is exactly the path Cloudflare described.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: File uploads: names, types, storage and execution
question: Why does OWASP say to apply the size limit after decompression for archives?
options: Compressed files are always safe
Decompression changes the file signature
Archives cannot contain executable files
A small compressed file can expand to an enormous size (a zip bomb) and fill disk or memory when the server unpacks it
explain: Compression ratios can be extreme, so a few kilobytes can become gigabytes. Limit the expanded size, using safe extraction code that counts bytes as it goes.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: HiCache: a radix tree that spans GPU, host memory and storage
question: Your host link is busy with L3 prefetch traffic, and most cached prefixes in your workload are used exactly once. Which write policy fits best?
options: write_through, so that every node already has a host copy when it is evicted
No HiCache at all: one-off prefixes can never benefit
write_back with a larger --hicache-ratio
write_through_selective, which copies a node only after it is hit again
explain: Selective write-through spends host bandwidth only on prefixes that proved reusable, so one-off prompts never cost a copy. Plain write_through copies everything, which wastes the busy link. write_back also skips copies until eviction, but then copies whatever is evicted, including one-off prefixes, on the eviction path.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Inside the server: three processes and an overlapped loop
question: Your server runs out of GPU memory during prefill of very long prompts, while decoding is fine. Which change do the docs suggest first?
options: Disable the radix cache
Switch the schedule policy to lpm
Lower `--chunked-prefill-size` (for example to 4096 or 2048)
Increase `--mem-fraction-static`
explain: Prefill activations scale with the number of tokens in one forward pass, and chunking caps it. Raising `--mem-fraction-static` would give the KV pool more memory and leave less for activations, making prefill OOM more likely.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: A*: steering the search with a lower bound
question: What does A* do if h(n) = 0 for every node?
options: It settles exactly the nodes plain Dijkstra settles, since f = g
It fails, because 0 is not a valid lower bound
It settles only the nodes on the shortest path
It becomes breadth-first search
explain: Zero never overestimates, so it is admissible, but it gives no guidance: f equals g and the queue order is Dijkstra's. The paper notes this trivial estimate satisfies the consistency assumption.

courseTitle: Signal processing basics: sampling, the FFT and filters
lessonTitle: The DFT: one dot product per complex sinusoid
question: x is a real signal of length 8 and its DFT has X[3] = 2 + 5i. What is X[5]?
options: 0, because only one of a pair can be nonzero
explain: For real input, X[N - k] is the complex conjugate of X[k]. Here N - 3 = 5, so X[5] = 2 - 5i. This symmetry is why rfft can skip the upper half of the bins without losing information.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: One instruction, many lanes: SIMD registers and lane counts
question: Which of these operations is horizontal rather than vertical?
options: out[i] = a[i] * b[i] for 8 lanes
out[i] = max(a[i], 0) for 8 lanes
Adding the 8 lanes of one register into a single total
Comparing a[i] > b[i] lane by lane
explain: A horizontal operation combines lanes of the same register. The other three only pair lane i with lane i, so they are vertical and cost one instruction each.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Arm Neon and SVE: fixed width versus length agnostic
question: Why can SVE vectorize strlen safely while a naive fixed-width SIMD strlen risks a crash?
options: SVE registers are wider
First-faulting loads record lanes that would fault in FFR instead of trapping
SVE checks string lengths in hardware
strlen is always auto-vectorized on Arm
explain: Reading a full vector past the terminating zero can cross into an unmapped page. ldff1 suppresses faults after the first active lane and marks which lanes loaded in FFR, so the loop processes only those and continues. Fixed-width code needs alignment tricks to avoid crossing pages.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: The buddy allocator: split in halves, merge with one XOR
question: A free block of order 2 starts at pfn 12. Where is its buddy, and if the buddy is also free, where does the merged order-3 block start?
options: Buddy at pfn 16; merged block starts at 12
Buddy at pfn 14; merged block starts at 12
Buddy at pfn 8; merged block starts at 8
Buddy at pfn 4; merged block starts at 4
explain: 12 in binary is 1100. Order 2 means flip bit 2 (value 4): 1100 XOR 0100 = 1000 = 8. The merged block starts at 12 AND 8 = 8, and covers pfn 8 to 15. Note that 16 is wrong: 12 to 19 would not be aligned to 8.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Placing training and rollout: colocated or separate GPUs
question: A colocated run runs out of GPU memory in SGLang right after the first training step, but rollout alone (`--debug-rollout-only`) is fine. Which knob does the usage guide point to first?
options: Increase `--rollout-num-gpus-per-engine`
Lower `--sglang-mem-fraction-static` so SGLang leaves room for Megatron's residual memory
Disable `--offload-train`
Switch `--ckpt-format` to torch
explain: Offloading is never perfect: Megatron keeps a few GB resident. The guide says that in colocated mode you must reduce SGLang's static memory fraction so both can coexist. Disabling train offload would make it worse.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Fully async rollout and the price of staleness
question: A teammate enables fully async rollout on a colocated 8-GPU job and sees no speedup. Why?
options: Fully async only works with PPO
The default --sglang-server-concurrency is too low
With colocation rollout and training share GPUs and must take turns, so there are no independent resources to overlap
Fully async requires delta weight sync
explain: The docs say fully async needs separate GPUs for meaningful overlap. On shared GPUs the phases still alternate, so the async bound does not apply.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Consensus under attack: Sybil, 51 percent and eclipse attacks
question: An attacker with 30 percent of the hash power is 6 blocks behind the honest chain. Using the catch-up formula, roughly how likely is the attacker to ever catch up?
options: About 0.6 percent
About 30 percent
About 2 in a million
Zero, 6 blocks is final
explain: (0.3/0.7)^6 is about 0.0062. That is the chance from a fixed 6-block deficit. A recipient waiting 6 confirmations faces worse odds, because the attacker mines in secret meanwhile: Nakamoto's full calculation gives about 13 percent at 30 percent and about 0.02 percent at 10 percent. So exchanges raise confirmations where hash power is cheap to rent.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Reentrancy: The DAO and checks-effects-interactions
question: A team says: 'Our withdraw uses a reentrancy guard, so we can update balances after the external call.' What is still at risk?
options: A different, unguarded function that reads the stale balance during the external call
Nothing: the guard blocks every reentry
Only gas costs
Signature replay
explain: A guard protects the functions that carry it. Cross-function reentrancy re-enters an unguarded function that trusts the not-yet-updated state. CEI removes the stale state itself.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Front-running, MEV and commit-reveal
question: Why does the commitment include msg.sender, not just hash(answer, salt)?
options: So another account cannot copy the commitment and later replay the same reveal as its own
To make the hash longer
Because keccak256 needs three inputs
To save gas
explain: Without the sender, Eve can submit Ana's commitment and, once Ana reveals, reveal the same answer and salt. Binding the address makes the commitment valid only for its author.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Keys, multisigs and blind signing: Bybit 2025
question: A Safe transaction to an unknown contract has operation = 1 and data that decodes as transfer(address,uint256). Why is that a red flag even though it 'looks like a transfer'?
options: With delegatecall, the target's code runs as the wallet and can write any storage slot, whatever the function is named
transfer is never allowed from a multisig
operation = 1 means the transaction is free
Function selectors are unique, so it must be a real token transfer
explain: A selector names a function, not what it does. Under delegatecall, the unknown contract's 'transfer' can overwrite the proxy's implementation slot, which is exactly what happened.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: What a SOC is, and what an analyst does all day
question: Which handover note is most useful to the next shift?
options: "Quiet night, a few alerts, all handled"
A list of every alert ID closed during the shift
"C-311: waiting on user reply since 05:40; if none by 09:00, revoke sessions. Proxy logs silent since 02:00, ticket P-88"
"Ask me if anything comes up"
explain: The next shift needs open items, what each is blocked on, the next step with a deadline, and environmental changes such as a dead log source. A list of closed IDs or a vague summary gives them nothing to act on, and the author may be asleep.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Suspicious logins: impossible travel and MFA push spam
question: Which single field most changes the urgency of a push-storm alert?
options: Whether a push was approved after the storm
The number of pushes
The user's department
The phone's operating system
explain: Many denied pushes mean the attacker has the password but not the account yet: urgent, but contained (reset the password). An approval after a storm means the attacker may already hold a session, so revoke it now and find out what it did.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Ransomware precursors, and deciding fast: Colonial Pipeline
question: At 02:14 a shadow-copy deletion alert fires on a file server. No other alerts yet. The on-call IR lead is asleep. What is the best first move?
options: Wait until the morning shift and investigate then
Restore the shadow copies
Email the server owner and wait for a reply
Page the IR lead now, isolate the host if the playbook pre-authorises it, and start collecting the process tree and the account that ran the command
explain: Recovery tampering is a late-stage precursor, and encryption may be minutes away. Paging at 02:14 is exactly what on-call exists for. Pre-authorised isolation buys time; evidence about the process and account tells IR how far the intrusion has spread.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: SOAR playbooks: what to automate and what to keep human
question: Which step is the best candidate for full automation with no human approval?
options: Disabling the CEO's account on a push-storm alert
Isolating a production database server on an EDR alert
Adding identity, asset owner and past-alert context to every new identity alert
Closing alerts whose destination IP has a benign reputation
explain: Enrichment is repetitive, fast and harmless if it errs: it only adds context for a human. The others are high-impact (CEO account, production database) or rely on reputation data that is easily wrong (lesson 5).

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Warnings people heed: browser warnings and opinionated design
question: Chrome's 2013 SSL warning had 70.2% clickthrough while its malware warning had 23.2%. What does Akhawe and Felt's comparison mostly show?
options: Chrome users are more reckless than Firefox users
The presentation and context of a warning strongly change behaviour
SSL errors are always harmless
Malware warnings are shown less often
explain: Chrome users heeded most malware warnings, and Firefox users heeded most SSL warnings. The large difference for one warning type in one browser points at that warning's design and context, not at the users.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Voice clones and deepfake meetings: when seeing is not believing
question: Why is a video call that the requester arranges weak evidence of identity, even if the faces look right?
options: Because the requester controls that channel, so its content can be fabricated end to end
Because video calls are always encrypted
Because faces cannot be seen clearly on video
Because video calls are not recorded
explain: In the Arup case every participant except the victim was generated. Evidence produced inside a channel the attacker set up proves nothing about identity; only an independent channel does.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Physical security in layers: zones, CPTED and access rules
question: A company removes the bushes outside its ground-floor windows and lights the car park. Which CPTED approach is that?
options: Territorial behaviour
Natural access control
Natural surveillance
Target hardening with locks
explain: Clearing sightlines and adding light lets people see and be seen, which is natural surveillance. Access control steers movement; territorial behaviour marks ownership.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Testing the people layer: rules of engagement, ethics and metrics
question: A phishing simulation's click rate falls from 12% to 6%, and its report rate falls from 40% to 15%. Which reading is best?
options: The programme is working, since fewer people click
Reporting has collapsed, which removes the early warning the SOC depends on; investigate why
Click rate is the only metric that matters
The lure was too easy
explain: Fewer clicks with far fewer reports can mean people ignore or delete suspicious mail out of fear or fatigue. The report is what lets responders contain a real campaign.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: The sparse autoencoder: a wide, sparse dictionary for activations
question: You train an SAE on layer 6 residual-stream activations of your GPT. Which statement is true?
options: The GPT's weights are updated so its neurons become monosemantic
The SAE has fewer hidden units than d_model so it compresses the activations
The SAE is trained on next-token cross-entropy only
The GPT is frozen; the SAE learns a wider, sparse re-description of the saved layer 6 vectors
explain: The SAE is a separate model trained on stored activations. It is overcomplete (M much larger than d) and trained with a reconstruction plus sparsity objective, not by changing the language model.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Measuring an SAE and steering a model with its features
question: Two SAEs on the same residual-stream layer: A has L0 = 40 and FVU = 0.30; B has L0 = 400 and FVU = 0.10. Which conclusion is justified from these numbers alone?
options: Neither dominates; compare them on the same L0 or the same FVU, and check delta LM loss
B is strictly better because its FVU is lower
A is strictly better because it is sparser
They must have the same downstream loss because they share a layer
explain: SAEs live on a sparsity versus fidelity frontier. B buys lower error with ten times more active latents. Fair comparisons hold one axis fixed, and downstream loss can rank SAEs differently from MSE.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Inverse distance weighting: weights from distance alone
question: You switch an IDW map from p = 1 to p = 6. What happens to the map?
options: It approaches nearest neighbor: flat patches around each sensor with sharper transitions between them
It becomes smoother everywhere
It starts extrapolating trends beyond the readings
Nothing, because weights are normalized
explain: A large power makes the nearest sensor dominate, so the map looks like Voronoi tiles with steeper transitions. Normalization keeps weights summing to 1, but it does not undo the change in their ratios.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Why decoding is slow and why checking guesses is cheap
question: Why can the target model score 5 guessed tokens in roughly the time it takes to generate 1 token at batch size 1?
options: The target skips attention for guessed tokens
Guessed tokens use a lower precision path
The GPU runs 5 separate copies of the model in parallel
At small batch the step is memory bound: weights and KV cache are read once either way, and 5 token vectors add little arithmetic
explain: The cost of a small-batch decode step is dominated by reading weights and KV cache from memory. Multiplying those weights by 5 vectors instead of 1 adds arithmetic the chip has to spare, so latency barely changes (Chen et al.'s argument for linear layers, attention and all-reduces).

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Build it: speculative sampling with two real models
question: After a rejection, an implementation forgets to roll back the target's KV cache and appends the next round's tokens after the stale entries. What happens?
options: It crashes with a shape mismatch on the next verify pass
Outputs stay correct, but each round wastes a few cache slots
Only sampling is affected; greedy output still matches the target
Outputs silently diverge: the target attends to rejected guesses as if they were text, at shifted positions, so its distributions are wrong
explain: Nothing checks that cache contents match the accepted text. The stale keys and values change every later attention result and push position indices forward. In our run all four greedy test outputs diverged from target.generate, two at the second token.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Self-speculation: MTP heads, layer skipping and lookahead
question: Which two methods need no extra parameters and no training at all?
options: Medusa-1 and EAGLE-3
MTP drafting and LayerSkip
Lookahead decoding and prompt lookup
DistillSpec and Medusa-2
explain: Lookahead builds its n-gram pool from the target's own Jacobi iterations, and prompt lookup copies n-grams from the context. Medusa and EAGLE train heads, MTP modules are trained with the model, LayerSkip retrains it, and DistillSpec trains the draft.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: CTC and wav2vec 2.0: training without frame-level alignments
question: A CTC model must output the word too. Which frame path collapses to too?
options: t o o
t t o o o
t o _ o
_ t o o _
explain: Merging repeats turns t o o, t t o o o and _ t o o _ into to (or _to_, then to). Only t o _ o keeps two separate o runs, because the blank breaks the run before merging. Removing the blank then gives too.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: The heap: free lists, chunk headers and where malloc gets memory
question: On 64-bit glibc, how many heap bytes does `malloc(25)` consume?
explain: request2size computes (25 + 8 + 15) rounded down to a multiple of 16 = 48. The 8-byte header pushes 25 bytes past the 32-byte minimum chunk, whose usable size is only 24.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: When RAM runs out: page cache, file mappings, swap and thrashing
question: A process maps a 2 GiB file with `MAP_PRIVATE`, writes to 10 of its pages, and exits. What happened to the file on disk?
options: The 10 modified pages were written back at exit
Nothing: private mappings are copy-on-write, so the stores went to private copies
The whole file was rewritten
The write faulted with SIGSEGV because file mappings are read-only
explain: MAP_PRIVATE creates a private copy-on-write mapping: the first store to each page copies it, and updates are not carried through to the file. Only MAP_SHARED stores reach the page cache page and, through write-back, the file.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Directional ablation: what erasing the refusal direction reveals
question: Arditi et al. compared two ways of removing the refusal direction. Option A subtracts the refusal vector (x minus r) at one layer. Option B ablates r-hat at every layer. Both bypassed refusal comparably. What is B's advantage on harmless prompts?
options: B is faster at inference
B also improves MMLU (a multiple-choice knowledge benchmark, lesson 5)
A shifts every activation by a fixed amount, pushing harmless ones far past zero; B only removes what is there, so it raised loss on harmless data less
There is no difference on harmless prompts
explain: Subtraction moves all activations by the same vector, so prompts with little refusal content end up strongly negative along r, an unnatural state. Ablation sets the component to zero regardless. In the paper's comparison, activation addition in the negative direction caused higher loss on harmless data than directional ablation.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Beyond one fixed vector: conditional, learned and monitoring uses
question: You want a coding assistant to refuse only questions about medical diagnosis and answer everything else normally. Which approach fits best?
options: CAST: a medical-diagnosis condition vector gates a refusal behavior vector
Add a refusal vector at every forward pass with a small coefficient
Ablate the refusal direction at every layer
LEACE on the refusal concept
explain: A fixed vector shifts every prompt, so a small one is too weak on medical prompts and still leaks into others. Ablation and LEACE remove refusal rather than adding it selectively. CAST checks the hidden state against a condition direction and applies the refusal vector only when the condition fires.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Windows, watermarks and allowed lateness, step by step
question: A Flink job reads a Kafka topic with 8 partitions. One partition stops receiving data. Per-minute windows stop producing results for all sensors. Why?
options: Kafka blocks all partitions when one is empty
Allowed lateness is too large
Tumbling windows require data in every partition
The operator's watermark is the minimum over its inputs, and the idle partition's watermark never advances
explain: Watermarks are tracked per partition and combined with a minimum. A silent partition pins the minimum, so no window end is ever passed. Marking idle inputs (withIdleness) lets the watermark advance without them.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Scaled dot-product attention, computed on four tokens
question: In the toy example, which statement about the attention weights of sat is correct?
options: sat attends most to itself because a token always matches its own key best
sat attends most to cat because q_sat dotted with k_cat = 2 is the largest score in its row
All four weights are equal because the values are different sizes
The weights depend on the value vectors
explain: Weights come only from query-key dot products: sat's row is (-1, 2, 1, 0) and the 2 belongs to cat. A token does not automatically match itself best, because W^Q and W^K are different matrices. Values only enter after the weights are fixed.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Relative positions: from sinusoids to RoPE and ALiBi
question: An ALiBi model has a head with slope 1/2 and a head with slope 1/256. Which one can still give a key 20 tokens back a weight comparable to the current token?
options: The slope-1/2 head, because steeper slopes reach further
Both equally, because the bias is the same for every head
Neither, because ALiBi masks keys more than 16 tokens back
The slope-1/256 head: its penalty at distance 20 is only about -0.08, against -10 for the other
explain: The penalty is slope times distance: 20 x 1/2 = 10 subtracted from the score, which shrinks that key's weight by a factor of e to the 10th (about 22,000), versus 20/256 = 0.078 for the shallow head. ALiBi biases scores; it does not mask distant keys.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Term-frequency saturation: what k1 controls
question: With k1 = 1.2 and average-length documents, doc P contains a term 2 times and doc Q contains it 20 times. Roughly how much larger is Q's factor than P's?
options: About 1.5 times larger (0.94 vs 0.62)
10 times larger
Exactly the same
About 3 times larger
explain: P: 2/(2+1.2) = 0.625. Q: 20/(21.2) = 0.943. The ratio is about 1.5, not 10. That is saturation: ten times the count gives about one and a half times the weight.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: BM25 in Lucene and Elasticsearch: fields, tuning, limits
question: An Elasticsearch index has 5 shards and a rare term that happens to be concentrated in one shard. Why might the same document get a slightly different BM25 score than in a single-shard index?
options: IDF and avgdl are computed from per-shard statistics by default
BM25 uses random tie-breaking
k1 is divided by the number of shards
Norms are only stored on the primary shard
explain: Lucene computes N, n_t and avgdl from the index it searches. In Elasticsearch each shard is a separate Lucene index, and the default query_then_fetch search type scores with local, per-shard term and document frequencies. Skewed terms then get different IDFs per shard. The dfs_query_then_fetch search type gathers global frequencies first, at extra cost.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Next-token prediction: turning raw text into training examples
question: A teammate's first logged loss on the 65-character model is 27. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The model is already overfitting
The data loader is shifting targets by two
The initialization makes some logits huge, so the model is confidently wrong
Nothing: 27 is typical for an untrained character model
explain: An untrained model with small weights should print about ln 65 = 4.17. A much larger loss means a very low probability on the true token, which only happens when logits are large and spread out, typically from weights initialized with too large a scale.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Training it: initialization, AdamW and a warmup plus cosine schedule
question: You start GPT-2 small at the peak rate 6e-4 with no warmup and the loss spikes to NaN within 100 steps. Which change addresses the cause most directly?
options: Increase weight decay to 1.0
Add a linear warmup over the first few thousand steps
Remove gradient clipping
Switch from cosine decay to a constant rate
explain: In the first steps Adam's running statistics are still settling, so full-size updates can blow up a freshly initialized model. Warmup ramps the step size meanwhile, which is why nanoGPT warms up for 2,000 steps. Xiong et al. find pre-LN models like GPT-2 less fragile here than post-LN ones, but warmup remains the standard fix. Removing clipping or raising decay does not touch the cause, and the decay shape only matters later.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Generating text: the sampling loop, temperature, top-k and top-p
question: A sampling script uses `logits[logits <= v[:, [-1]]] = -inf` (note `<=`) with top_k = 5. What happens?
options: Nothing changes; < and <= behave the same
The 5th-largest logit (and any ties with it) is also removed, so only 4 tokens survive; with top_k = 1 every logit is masked and softmax returns NaN
Top-k now keeps 6 tokens
Temperature stops having an effect
explain: v[:, [-1]] is the k-th largest logit, the threshold that must survive. With <= it is thrown away too, leaving k - 1 choices, and for k = 1 nothing survives: all minus infinity gives NaN probabilities and multinomial fails.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: The multivariable chain rule: summing over every path
question: $f = x y + x$ with $x = 2$, $y = 5$. What is $\partial f / \partial x$?
options: 5, from the product term only
6: the path through the product gives y = 5 and the added x gives 1
1, from the added x only
7, which is x + y
explain: $x$ reaches $f$ by two paths. Through $xy$ the local rate is $y = 5$; through the bare $+ x$ term it is 1. The paths add: $5 + 1 = 6$. Keeping only one path is the fan-out mistake.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Backpropagation: the chain rule run backward through a graph
question: A model has 1 million parameters. Roughly how many forward evaluations of the loss does a centered finite-difference gradient need, compared with backprop?
options: About 2, the same as backprop
About 2 million, versus one forward plus one backward pass for backprop
About 1000, the square root of the parameter count
Exactly 1 million, versus 1 million backward passes for backprop
explain: Centered differences need two evaluations per parameter, $2 \times 10^6$ forward passes. Reverse-mode differentiation gets the whole gradient of a scalar loss from one forward and one backward pass, which is why finite differences are only used to spot-check gradients.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Writing scripts: arguments, tests, if, loops and functions
question: After `f() { echo 5; return 3; }` and `y=$(f)`, what are y and `$?`?
options: y is 5 and `$?` is 3
y is 3 and `$?` is 0
y is 5 and `$?` is 0
y is 53 and `$?` is 0
explain: Command substitution captures what f prints, 5. The return value is not output; it becomes the exit status, and an assignment whose value came from `$(...)` takes that command's status, 3 (a real bash run printed `y=5 status=3`).

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Exit statuses and scripts that fail loudly
question: A CI step runs `pytest | tee test.log` (tee copies its input to the screen and to a file) and always shows green even when tests fail. What is the minimal fix?
options: Replace `|` with `&&`
Add `set -u`
Add `set -o pipefail` before the command
Redirect with `2>&1` instead of piping
explain: The pipeline's status is tee's, which succeeds. pipefail makes the pipeline report the rightmost non-zero status, so pytest's failure surfaces. `&&` would stop tee from seeing the output stream at all.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Learning word vectors by predicting their neighbours
question: A balanced binary tree holds a vocabulary of $W = 1{,}048{,}576 = 2^{20}$ words at its leaves. How many sigmoid decisions does hierarchical softmax make to score one word?
explain: The path from the root to a leaf in a balanced tree of $2^{20}$ leaves has 20 inner nodes, one sigmoid each, instead of a million dot products. A Huffman tree is not balanced: frequent words get shorter paths and rare words longer ones, which lowers the average cost on real text.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Embeddings for IDs: categorical features, hashing and weight tying
question: Your product catalog adds thousands of new item IDs every day, and the model uses one learned embedding row per ID. What problem should you expect for brand-new items?
options: Their rows are still at their random initialization because they have received no gradient, so their similarities are meaningless
None, embeddings generalize to any ID
They will all collapse to the zero vector
Their vectors will equal the average of all rows
explain: A row learns only when its ID appears in training. New IDs keep their random initial vectors (in PyTorch drawn from N(0, 1)). Systems handle this cold-start problem with a shared unknown or hashed row, or by building vectors from content features, the same idea fastText uses with character n-grams in the next lesson.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Contrastive training in practice: in-batch negatives and collapse
question: Which of these objectives is minimized by an encoder that maps every image to the same vector?
options: Alignment alone, $\mathcal{L}_{\text{align}}$
NT-Xent with in-batch negatives
Uniformity, $\mathcal{L}_{\text{uniform}}$
MoCo's loss with a queue of negatives
explain: A constant encoder puts every positive pair at distance 0, the minimum of alignment. Every loss that includes negatives or a uniformity term penalizes it: NT-Xent costs ln(2N - 1) per row, and uniformity reaches its maximum, 0.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Fewer bytes per weight: number formats and weight-only quantization
question: LLaMA-7B moves from FP16 to INT4 weight-only quantization on an A100. Roughly what happens to the time to first token for a 4,000-token prompt?
options: It drops about 4x, like the decode floor
Almost nothing: prefill needs about 53.6 TFLOP, about 172 ms of math, and weight reads (6.6 ms in FP16) were already hidden under it
It doubles, because dequantizing costs extra FLOPs
It drops 2x, because INT4 math is twice as fast
explain: Prefill of 4,000 tokens is $2\times6.7\times10^9\times4000\approx53.6$ TFLOP, about 172 ms at 312 TFLOP/s. Reading the weights took only 6.6 ms in FP16 and is overlapped with that math. Weight-only INT4 still computes in 16-bit, so the math is unchanged. Speeding up prefill needs low-precision compute (W8A8, FP8).

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: From hello.c to a running process
question: You split a program into `main.c` and `util.c`. `main.c` calls `parse()` defined in `util.c`. Which stage is the first one that needs to see both files?
options: The preprocessor, because it must find parse()
The compiler, because it must check parse() exists
The assembler, because it encodes the call instruction
The linker, because it resolves the call to parse() across object files
explain: Each .c file is preprocessed, compiled and assembled on its own; a declaration of `parse` (usually from a header) is enough for the compiler. The call is left as an undefined symbol plus a relocation in main.o. The linker is the first stage that sees both object files and patches the real address in.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Where a program's memory lives: code, heap and stack
question: Right after `call square` executes, which statement is true?
options: rsp increased by 8 and the program counter points at square
rsp is unchanged; the return address is kept in a special register
rsp decreased by 8, the stack top holds the address of the instruction after the call, and the program counter points at square
rsp decreased by 8 and the stack top holds the address of square
explain: The stack grows down, so a push subtracts 8 from rsp. call pushes the return address (the next instruction in the caller), not the target, then jumps by writing square's address into the program counter.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Virtual memory: every process gets its own addresses
question: Why does x86-64 use a 4-level tree instead of one flat table indexed by the 36-bit page number?
options: A flat table cannot be cached in the TLB
Flat tables cannot hold physical frame numbers
Hardware cannot index arrays larger than 512 entries
A flat table would need 2^36 entries x 8 bytes = 512 GiB per process, mostly describing unused memory
explain: 2^36 x 8 bytes = 512 GiB (a gibibyte is 2^30 bytes), for every process. A tree only allocates the lower-level tables for regions actually in use, so a small process needs a few pages of page tables. The cost is the longer walk, which the TLB hides.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Supervised fine-tuning: same loss, curated data, masked prompt
question: Why must the end-of-sequence token after the answer be included in the trained targets?
options: It carries the reward signal for RLHF
It is required by the softmax
Otherwise the model never learns when to stop and keeps generating
It prevents the prompt from being masked
explain: Stopping is a learned prediction like any other. If the end token is masked, the model never sees a gradient for ending its turn and tends to run on, for example by writing the next user turn itself.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: RL with PPO: maximize reward, stay close to the SFT model
question: In a PPO minibatch, a token has advantage -0.5 and its ratio has fallen to 0.7, with epsilon 0.2. What does this token contribute to the gradient?
options: A push to lower its probability further, because its advantage is negative
A push to raise its probability back to 1
Nothing, because negative advantages are always clipped
Nothing: the clipped term -0.4 is the minimum and does not depend on the weights
explain: rho x A = -0.35 and clip(0.7, 0.8, 1.2) x A = -0.4. The min is the clipped -0.4, a constant, so no gradient flows: the token was already made 30 percent less likely, past the 20 percent PPO allows per batch. If its ratio had been 1.3 instead, the unclipped -0.65 would be the min and the gradient would push it back down.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Analysis in depth: tokenizing, stemming and what normalizing costs
question: Index and queries both go through lowercase, split on spaces, then Porter. Which query word matches d6 (*the miss rate fell after the roll back*) only because of stemming?
options: falls, because Porter maps both fell and falls to fall
hotter, because Porter strips the comparative ending
rates, because Porter maps rates to rate
skipped, because Porter maps it to a stem that d6 contains
explain: Lucene's Porter filter gives rates to rate, which d6 contains. falls becomes fall but fell stays fell: an irregular verb needs a lemmatizer. hotter stays hotter, and skipped becomes skip, which d6 does not contain. missing (to miss) and rolled (to roll) would also match d6 after stemming.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Ranking with vectors and cosine similarity
question: Why do engines store the integer tf in each posting instead of the final tf-idf weight?
options: Because idf depends on df and N, which change as documents are added, and an integer is cheaper to store than a float
Because floats cannot be sorted
Because tf-idf weights are always integers anyway
Because cosine similarity ignores idf
explain: idf is a collection-wide statistic, so a stored tf-idf float would go stale every time the collection changes. A small integer tf also compresses far better than a float. The engine combines tf with the current idf at query time.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Multi-file C: headers, include guards, static, extern and make
question: util.c defines `static int helper(void) { ... }`. main.c declares `int helper(void);` and calls it. What happens?
options: It builds and runs, because the prototype matches
Compile error in util.c
Compile error in main.c, because helper is static
Link error: no definition of helper is visible to main.o
explain: Each file compiles: main.c only needs the declaration. But static gives util.c's helper internal linkage, so it is not exported to the linker, and main.o's reference to helper finds no definition. Clang on macOS reported `Undefined symbols ... "_helper", referenced from: _main in m.o`.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Object lifetimes: automatic, static and malloc'd memory
question: Which of these functions returns a pointer that the caller can safely use after the function returns?
options: int *f(void) { int n = 1; return &n; }
int *g(void) { int a[3] = {0}; return a; }
int *h(void) { int *p = malloc(sizeof *p); if (p) *p = 1; return p; }
All three, because the bytes are still in memory
explain: f and g return the address of automatic objects (g's array decays to a pointer to a[0]), whose lifetime ends at return. h returns allocated storage, which lives until free, so the caller may use it and is responsible for freeing it.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Undefined behavior, and the tools that catch it
question: Which of these operations has fully defined behavior in standard C?
options: int x = INT_MAX; x = x + 1;
unsigned u = UINT_MAX; u = u + 1;
int a[5]; int y = a[5];
free(p); free(p);
explain: Unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo 2 to the power of the bit width, so u becomes 0. Signed overflow, reading one past the end of an array, and freeing twice are all undefined behavior.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Who frees this memory? Ownership and drop
question: Three local variables `x`, `y`, `z` (declared in that order) all implement `Drop`. In what order do their `drop` methods run at the end of the block?
options: x, y, z
Unspecified; it depends on the optimizer
z, y, x
explain: Locals are dropped in reverse order of declaration, as specified in the Rust Reference. This is deterministic, not up to the optimizer.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Slices and why references cannot dangle
question: Why does returning `&s[0..5]` from `first_word` prevent the clear-then-use bug, when returning the index 5 did not?
options: Slices are copied, so clearing `s` does not affect them
The slice is a borrow of `s`, so any `&mut s` (like `clear`) while it is still used is a compile error
`clear` checks at run time whether slices exist
explain: The borrow checker tracks the slice as a shared borrow of `s`. `clear` needs a mutable borrow, and shared XOR mutable makes the overlap illegal. There is no run-time check involved.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: A vector is a list of numbers and an arrow at the same time
question: An embedding $\mathbf{v} = [0.6, 0.8]$ is multiplied by the scalar $-2$. What happens to it as an arrow?
options: It points the opposite way and its length becomes 2
It rotates 90 degrees and keeps its length
It points the opposite way and its length becomes -2
It keeps its direction and its length becomes 2
explain: $-2\mathbf{v} = [-1.2, -1.6]$, whose norm is $\sqrt{1.44+2.56} = 2$. The minus sign flips the direction; lengths are never negative, so the length is $|{-2}| \times 1 = 2$. Scaling never rotates by anything other than 0 or 180 degrees.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Matrix multiplication: composing maps and checking shapes
question: You need $ABx$ where $A$ and $B$ are $1000 \times 1000$ and $x$ is a vector. Which order of evaluation is cheaper?
options: (AB)x, because multiplying matrices first is faster
A(Bx), because two matrix-vector products cost about 2 million multiply-adds versus about 1 billion for AB
They cost the same because multiplication is associative
Neither; you must invert A first
explain: Associativity guarantees the same answer, not the same cost. $AB$ alone is $1000^3 = 10^9$ multiply-adds. $B\mathbf{x}$ then $A(B\mathbf{x})$ is $2 \times 1000^2 = 2\times10^6$.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: The SVD: rotate, stretch, rotate, then keep what matters
question: PCA on centered 2D data gives singular values 9 and 3. What share of the variance does the first component capture?
options: 75 percent
90 percent
81 percent
97 percent
explain: Variance shares use squared singular values: $81/(81 + 9) = 0.9$. 75 percent comes from using $9/(9+3)$ without squaring.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Many features: linear regression in matrix form and feature scaling
question: $X$ has 500 rows (examples) and 20 columns (19 features plus the ones column). What is the shape of $\nabla L = \frac{2}{n}X^\top(Xw - y)$?
options: 500 by 1, one entry per example
20 by 20, like the Hessian
20 by 1, one partial derivative per weight
500 by 20, like X
explain: $Xw - y$ has one residual per example (500). $X^\top$ is 20 by 500, so the product has 20 entries: one partial derivative for each of the 20 weights, including the bias. The 20 by 20 matrix is $X^\top X$, which appears in the Hessian and the normal equations.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Validation and penalties: choosing lambda, L2 and L1
question: You fit a lasso on 200 features and 180 of the learned weights come out exactly 0. What is the most reasonable reading?
options: The solver failed to converge
The L1 penalty judged those 180 features not worth their cost, so the model uses only 20
L1 always zeroes 90 percent of the weights
The features must have been standardized wrongly
explain: Exact zeros are what L1 is for: its constant-size pull pins weak weights at 0, giving a sparse model that effectively selects 20 features. How many survive depends on alpha, chosen on validation data. L2 would have kept all 200 small but nonzero.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Data pitfalls: leakage, distribution shift and baselines
question: Before splitting, you fill missing values in a column with the mean of the whole dataset. Is that leakage?
options: No, means are harmless
Only if the column is the label
Yes: the fill value used held-out rows; compute it on the training fold only
Only for time series
explain: Imputation is a fitted preprocessing step like scaling. Its fill value should be learned from training rows and reused for validation and test. The effect is usually small for a mean, but the habit matters, and a Pipeline makes it automatic.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: The forward pass: layers as matrix multiplies
question: In the convention $z^l = W^l a^{l-1} + b^l$, what is the shape of $W^2$ for that 784-100-10 network?
explain: $W^l$ has one row per unit in layer $l$ and one column per unit in layer $l-1$: 10 output units by 100 hidden units.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: The cost of backprop: compute, activation memory, checkpointing
question: You double the batch size and the run now goes out of GPU memory, even though the model's weights are unchanged. What is the most likely cause?
options: The weights are copied once per example
Backprop needs a second copy of the loss
Stored activations for the backward pass scale with batch size
Gradients scale with batch size while weights do not, and gradients are the bulk
explain: Weights and their gradients have a fixed size. Activations kept for the backward pass scale with batch size times depth, so they grow. Remedies: a smaller batch, gradient checkpointing (recompute instead of store), or lower precision activations.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Processes and limited direct execution
question: Why must the instruction that installs the trap table be privileged?
options: Because it is slow and should run only at boot
Because the trap table is stored on disk
Because a user process could otherwise point system calls and interrupts at its own code and take over the machine
Because user programs do not know the system-call numbers
explain: The trap table decides which code runs in kernel mode on every trap and interrupt. If a user program could install its own, it would run arbitrary code with full privilege, defeating all protection. So, like starting the timer, it is restricted to kernel mode.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Concurrency: race conditions and locks
question: On a single CPU with a non-preemptive scheduler (no timer switches), Thread 2 calls a spin lock held by Thread 1. What happens?
options: Thread 2 acquires the lock after one time slice
Thread 2 spins forever: Thread 1 never gets the CPU back to release the lock
The lock automatically turns into a sleeping lock
Thread 1 releases the lock because spinning causes an interrupt
explain: A spinning thread never gives up the CPU on its own. Without preemption, the holder never runs again, so the lock is never released. OSTEP points out that spin locks need a preemptive scheduler to work correctly on a single processor.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Persistence: how a hard disk spends its time
question: Why can SSTF (shortest seek time first) starve a request?
options: Because it ignores rotation time
Because the OS does not know the disk's geometry
Because a steady stream of requests near the head always wins, so a request far away may never be served
Because it serves requests in arrival order
explain: SSTF always picks the closest request. If new nearby requests keep arriving, the far one is never closest. The elevator (SCAN) algorithm fixes this by sweeping in one direction, so every request is reached within a sweep. Ignoring rotation is a real weakness of both, but it is not the cause of starvation.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Probability by counting outcomes, and what conditioning does
question: A model's training set has 1,000 emails: 300 are spam, and 240 of the spam emails contain the word "free". Of the 700 non-spam emails, 70 contain "free". What is P(spam | contains "free")?
options: 0.80, because 240 of 300 spam emails contain free
0.24, because 240 of 1,000 emails are spam with free
About 0.77, because 240 of the 310 emails containing free are spam
0.30, the base rate of spam
explain: Condition on the event you observed: restrict to the 240 + 70 = 310 emails containing "free", of which 240 are spam, so 240/310 = 0.774. Option A is P(free | spam), the reverse conditional, a very common mix-up that the next lesson is about.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Continuous variables: densities, CDFs and common distributions
question: X is uniform on [0, 0.5]. Which statement is true?
options: Its density cannot exceed 1, so it is 1 on the interval
P(X = 0.25) = 2, the density there
Its density is 2 on the interval, and P(0.1 <= X <= 0.2) = 0.2
P(0.1 <= X <= 0.2) = 0.1, the length of the range
explain: The area must be 1 over a width of 0.5, so the height is 2. A range probability is width times height: 0.1 x 2 = 0.2. The length alone (0.1) is only right when the density is 1, and any single exact value has probability 0.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Entropy, cross-entropy and KL divergence
question: A language model's average cross-entropy on a test set is 2.0 nats per token. What is its perplexity?
options: About 7.4
About 0.14
explain: Perplexity is e to the cross-entropy in nats: e^2 = 7.39, as uncertain as choosing among about 7.4 equally likely tokens at each step. 4.0 would be 2 raised to 2.0, which is right only if the 2.0 were measured in bits.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Why loss falls on a straight line in log-log space
question: On log-log axes, a team's loss-versus-parameters points lie on a straight line with slope -0.07. Which statement is correct?
options: Each doubling of N removes the same fraction of the loss
Each doubling of N removes the same absolute amount of loss
Loss will reach zero at a finite model size
The slope says how much data the model needs
explain: A straight line in log-log space is a power law: equal multiplicative steps in N give equal multiplicative changes in L, here $2^{-0.07} \approx 0.95$ per doubling. Absolute drops shrink, the curve never reaches zero, and the slope says nothing about data needs on its own.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Kaplan vs Chinchilla: why 2020-era models were undertrained
question: GPT-3 used about 3.2e+23 FLOPs. Using $C \approx 6ND$ and Chinchilla's 20 tokens per parameter, what would a compute-optimal model at that budget look like?
options: 175B parameters on 300B tokens
About 500B parameters on 105B tokens
About 12B parameters on 4.3T tokens
About 51B parameters on 1.0T tokens
explain: Set $D = 20N$, so $C = 6 \cdot N \cdot 20N = 120N^2$ and $N = \sqrt{C/120} \approx 51$B, $D \approx 1.0$T. GPT-3's actual 175B on 300B tokens is the Kaplan-style choice; 12B on 4.3T overshoots the token ratio badly.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Building your own test set: queries, guidelines, pools and LLM judges
question: You will compare a BM25 baseline with a new reranker that uses the same LLM you plan to use as a judge. What must you do before trusting LLM labels for this comparison?
options: Nothing; LLM labels agree with humans as well as humans agree with each other
Use a larger LLM as the judge, which removes any bias
Judge only the reranker's results with the LLM and BM25's with humans
Have humans judge a sample that includes both systems' top results, and check LLM-human agreement on it
explain: The risk is that the judge rewards a system for agreeing with itself, which overall agreement numbers would not reveal.
